car102.desc: This high-performance variant of the seventh-generation Skyline was introduced with Group A competition squarely in its sights. Its RB20DET engine was extensively reworked, featuring a stainless steel exhaust manifold and a T04E turbocharger, complemented by refinements to the suspension and a more aggressive exterior design. The car secured the 1989 All Japan Touring Car Championship season title, yet it sparked curiosity as to why it wasn't given the GT-R name.
car102.hero: An unlikely monster machine born from the elegant lines of the seventh-generation Skyline.

car1027.desc: Formerly a vice president at GM, John Z. DeLorean struck out on his own to establish DeLorean Motor Company (DMC). The company’s first and only production model, the DMC-12, stood out with its bold stainless-steel body. Its signature gullwing doors quickly made it an icon, but despite its distinctive styling, the company went bankrupt in 1983. The owner of the newly reformed DMC, now dedicated to servicing and restoring original DeLoreans, answered the call from fans by releasing the Series 2 DeLorean, equipped with a 197.2 HP powerplant.
car1027.hero: At the request of DeLorean owners, the tuned-up Series 2 was created.

car104.desc: The 180SX was introduced as the liftback version of the S13 Silvia. Although it carried slightly more weight and had reduced rear-end rigidity compared to the Silvia, it quickly gained a following as aftermarket tuning parts became widely available. One of the most iconic customizations was the combination of the 180SX body with the front end of the Silvia, also known as “Sileighty.”
car104.hero: This Nissan blended the 180SX with the appealing front end of the Silvia.

car1040.desc: This LM-spec machine represented a Le Mans–style reinterpretation of the Ford GT—an evolution of the 1960s GT40 legacy, infused with modern technology. Under the rear deck sat a supercharged 5.4-liter DOHC V-8 producing 591.7 HP. It also featured a double wishbone suspension and a race-ready 6-speed gearbox.
car1040.hero: Gran Turismo commemorates the return of the legendary Le Mans-winning machine by offering its own interpretation.
car1040.nameLong: Ford GT LM Race Car Spec II
car1040.nameShort: Ford GT LM Race Car Spec II

car1044.desc: The Toyota Sports 800, affectionately known as the “Yota-Hachi,” was a compact sports car distinguished by its fixed B-pillar Targa-style removable roof panel. Extensive use of aluminum and acrylic throughout the body kept its weight down to just 1279 lbs. While its 750 cc engine produced a modest 44.4 HP, the car’s featherlight construction allowed it to reach a top speed of 96.3 mph—comparable to many 1.500 cc-class vehicles of its era.
car1044.hero: With its wide tread and low center of gravity, the "Yota-Hachi" was a capable sports car.

car105.desc: The 205 Turbo 16 itself was Peugeot’s Group B contender for the World Rally Championship. It won three rallies in its 1984 debut and repeated the feat in 1985. Peugeot evolved the car with more power, less weight, and better aerodynamics to produce the Evolution 2. The updated version captured 7 of 12 victories in 1985 and 6 of 13 in 1986, taking both the drivers' and manufacturers' titles.
car105.hero: This 4-wheel-drive pocket rocket took the Group B racing world by storm.

car1067.desc: Following its string of successes at Le Mans during the 1950s, Jaguar made a return to endurance racing in 1986 with a Group C prototype. Jaguar reached its peak in 1988 with the XJR-9. Thanks to its exceptional aerodynamics and durability, it claimed victory at the 24 Hours of Le Mans. That triumph secured its place in motorsports history, as Jaguar dethroned Porsche, the long-reigning champions of Le Mans.
car1067.hero: This iconic race car brought Jaguar many victories, notably against turbocharged competitors.

car1069.desc: The Chaparral 2J was a highly unconventional race car that competed in the 1970 SCCA Can-Am series. Nicknamed the “vacuum cleaner,” it featured a groundbreaking design with two fans mounted at the rear of the car. Powered by a separate secondary engine, these fans created powerful suction by extracting air from beneath the chassis. In effect, it became the world’s first active ground-effect race car. However, for the 1971 season, a change in SCCA regulations banned the use of auxiliary engines, leading to the retirement of the 2J.
car1069.hero: Dubbed by some as "the vacuum cleaner," this car became an American racing icon.

car116.desc: In 1998, Toyota developed the GT-One (TS020) with the singular goal of winning the 24 Hours of Le Mans. Designed by André de Cortanze, the car incorporated Formula 1-inspired aerodynamics and suspension. Although mechanical issues prevented a result in its debut year, the GT-One returned in 1999 as an evolved LM GTP machine. Ukyo Katayama and company finished 2nd overall—the highest-ever at Le Mans for a team composed entirely of Japanese drivers.
car116.hero: Toyota's endurance race machine that achieved a class win at Le Mans in 1999.

car135.desc: Honda’s lineage of sports cars began in 1963 with the ultra-compact, two-seat S500. It was followed by the S600, which delivered more power through a larger engine, and then by the S800, which featured 4-wheel independent suspension. Equipped with a more robust engine than the S600 and a short-throw shift lever positioned within easy reach of its low-slung seats, the S800 earned international praise.
car135.hero: With a larger displacement than its predecessor, this car represented the pinnacle of the "S" line.

car1365.desc: Although derived from the "Le Mans quattro" concept, the production version of this sports car took its name from Audi’s R8 race cars, which had earned a solid reputation with dominant performances at Le Mans. Built around Audi’s ultra-lightweight aluminum space frame, the car featured a 4.2-liter V-8 producing 414.2 HP, delivering power to all four wheels via the quattro system, which employed viscous couplings. In 2009, the lineup was expanded with the addition of the 5.2 FSI model, powered by a 5.2-liter V-10 generating 517.7 HP.
car1365.hero: Engineered to the finest detail, this Audi supercar features welds measured in microns.

car137.desc: Launched in 1991, the Honda Beat helped spark the boom in lightweight two-seat sports cars. Tipping the scales at just 1675 lbs, it also delivered near-perfect balance with a 43:57 front-to-rear weight ratio. Its engine, infused with F1-derived technology and paired with a short-stroke transmission, delivered a driving experience like no other. And you didn’t need mountain roads to enjoy it—the Beat brought pure sports car fun to your everyday drive.
car137.hero: This wonderful kei sports car offered style and driving excitement never before seen in Japan.

car1370.desc: This was the hot hatch version of the new MINI developed after BMW’s takeover. Its 1.6-liter inline-4 was supercharged to produce 167.7 HP and 159.1 ft-lb of torque, an increase of 53.3 HP and 50.6 ft-lb over the base Cooper. Paired with an exclusive 6-speed manual transmission, the car delivered pure driving fun in a compact, spirited package.
car1370.hero: This hopped-up MINI Cooper S featured a supercharged engine.

car1373.desc: This coupe was developed to fully exploit the Viper’s performance potential. While its basic structure, suspension, and V-10 engine remained largely unchanged from the RT/10 roadster, power output was increased to 449.7 HP. The addition of a fixed roof allowed the car to reach a top speed of 185 mph—approximately 183.9 mph—surpassing the roadster’s 165-mph limit. Introduced alongside it, the GTS-R race version appeared in endurance events across the globe, where it consistently demonstrated its superior capabilities.
car1373.hero: With its monstrous levels of power and grip, this venerable machine could arguably be called America's first supercar.

car1378.desc: The Ferrari F430 was a mid-engine V-8 supercar that made its debut in 2004. The newly developed 4.3-liter V-8 engine produced 483.2 HP. The chassis was developed from the 360 Modena, with key improvements in stability and aerodynamic downforce, constructed using Extra Super Duralumin aluminum alloy. This top-tier sports car reached a top speed of 195.7 mph and was available with carbon-ceramic brakes.
car1378.hero: The rolling piece of mechanical art was capable of reaching a top speed of 195.7 mph.

car1384.desc: An enhanced version of the Z33 Fairlady Z arrived in 2007. At its heart was the new VQ35HR engine, which raised output to 308.7 HP. A redesigned intake manifold and reduced internal friction refined the engine’s character, especially at high revs. Revised suspension settings further contributed to a flatter, more composed ride, while maintaining the car’s trademark agility.
car1384.hero: This refined Z33 model came powered by the next-generation VQ35HR engine.

car1385.desc: The Suzuki Swift Sport was the performance-focused variant of the second-generation Swift. At its heart was a naturally-aspirated 1.6-liter engine, tuned for high-revs and equipped with forged pistons and variable valve timing. A minor update in 2007 raised the rev limit from 7000 rpm to 7500 rpm. Paired with a close-ratio 5-speed manual gearbox, it delivered an exhilarating driving experience.
car1385.hero: Suzuki's fun-to-drive Swift Sport was made even more lively with a high-revving engine and close-ratio gears.

car1399.desc: Across multiple generations of the 3 Series, the M3 has consistently been positioned as a high-performance variant with a deep motorsports heritage. The E92 M3 paired a 7-speed dual-clutch transmission (DCT) with a high-revving 4.0-liter V-8 delivering 414.2 HP. Despite its larger body, extensive weight-saving measures kept the road car’s weight down to just 3593 lbs. It could sprint from zero to 62.1 mph in 4.8 seconds.
car1399.hero: Based on the E92 3 Series coupe, this 4th-gen M3 featured a 414.2 HP V8.

car140.desc: The 2000 All Japan Grand Touring Championship (JGTC) GT500 class saw fierce competition among Japan’s top three automakers: Honda, Toyota, and Nissan. That year, five teams fielded the NSX. They included the Castrol MUGEN NSX and Takata Dome NSX, running as official factory entries. While the Takata Dome NSX demonstrated remarkable potential, it was the Castrol MUGEN NSX, featured here, that claimed the championship. Its success came through strategic management of the weight handicaps, showcasing speed and discipline over the course of the season.
car140.hero: A new design with a lower center of gravity was the key to victory for this JGTC champion.

car1402.desc: This coupe was introduced during the Viper’s second generation, marking the car’s continued evolution as a true sports machine. It also carried the SRT badge, a symbol shared across many of Chrysler’s high-performance offerings. With its lightweight body and an 8.3-liter V-10 producing 509.9 HP, the car possessed the performance to compete against its international rivals.
car1402.hero: The much-anticipated fixed-roof version of the supercar featured better aerodynamics and lighter weight.

car1409.desc: This special model was created to commemorate the 40th anniversary of Ferrari’s founding. Developed using the same construction techniques as the race cars of its era, it featured a steel tubular frame combined with composite materials, including carbon-Kevlar and aluminum honeycomb structures. Its powerplant was derived from the twin-turbocharged V-8 used in the 288 GTO, tuned to produce 478.3 HP and 419.5 ft-lb of torque. This car would become the final road-going project overseen by Enzo Ferrari, and it continues to enjoy enduring admiration around the world.
car1409.hero: This special exotic machine was the last one produced under the guidance of company founder Enzo Ferrari.

car1410.desc: This modified version of Ferrari’s 365 GT4/BB was notable for being the brand’s first mid-engine 12-cylinder road car. The most significant revision was the enlargement of the engine to 5.0 liters; however, due to emissions regulations, power output was reduced by 19.7 HP, bringing the total to 355 HP. Torque was increased by 28.9 ft-lb, resulting in a formidable 332.7 ft-lb. One of Ferrari’s most iconic creations, this car—along with Lamborghini’s Countach—came to symbolize the exotic Italian supercars of the 1970s.
car1410.hero: One of the cars that defined the supercar boom in the 1970s, this car was considered the world's fastest, along with the Lamborghini Countach.

car1425.desc: This LM-spec race car took the 2004 Ford GT and reengineered it for the rigors of Le Mans competition. Power output was raised from the street version’s 550.3 HP to 591.7 HP, while the body—faithful in size and shape to the production GT—was reconstructed entirely in carbon fiber, bringing curb weight down to just 2535 lbs.
car1425.hero: Gran Turismo commemorates the return of the legendary Le Mans-winning machine by offering its own interpretation.
car1425.nameLong: Ford GT LM Spec II Test Car
car1425.nameShort: Ford GT LM Spec II Test Car

car1426.desc: Built to commemorate Ford’s 100th anniversary, the Ford GT drew both its silhouette and spirit from the iconic GT40—a legend born from its sweep of the top three positions at the 1966 24 Hours of Le Mans, and its unprecedented four-year winning streak that followed through 1969. With a 0–60 mph time of just 3.3 seconds and a top speed of 205.1 mph, the GT delivered performance worthy of its heritage. A total of 4,038 units were produced over a three-year span, concluding in 2006.
car1426.hero: The final-year model of this potent supercar came right after the company's 100th anniversary.

car1427.desc: Created by Mine’s, the BNR34 GT-R N1 base is a finely tuned expression of the R34 GT-R’s purity, capturing its beauty while remaining true to the spirit of a street car. From the refined RB26DETT engine to the lowered suspension and understated exterior, every detail reflected the philosophy of Mine’s CEO, Michizo Niikura — to create “a first-class street car.” This example was fully restored in 2021 by Garage Yoshida.
car1427.hero: This legendary, fully tuned GT-R gained a new following after an ambitious restoration.

car1431.desc: The Amemiya µ Boost up 7 was a street machine built by RE Amemiya, the legendary rotary tuner known for their presence in Super GT and D1GP. This car was engineered to fully exploit the FD3S platform’s capabilities as a cornering specialist. Celebrated for its performance on winding roads, it was featured in the Japanese DVD magazine Hot Version, where it earned the nickname “demon-lord of mountain paths” for its unmatched speed.
car1431.hero: The Amemiya FD3S was another stylish RX-7 created by master tuner, RE Amemiya.

car1433.desc: While Power House Amuse was well known for tuning the S2000, its most refined build was the S2000 GT1. Its body kit was constructed with carbon fiber developed in collaboration with Polyphony Digital. Despite an increase in width to 72.0 inches, the car’s overall weight dropped to around 2469 lbs. Performance was further enhanced with engine upgrades, resulting in a remarkable power-to-weight ratio of just 4 lbs per 1 horsepower.
car1433.hero: Development engineers of Gran Turismo contributed with Amuse to build this ultimate S2000.

car1448.desc: The seventh-generation S15 Silvia marked a return to the more compact proportions of the S13, reestablishing itself as an accessible, rear-wheel-drive sports car. While it continued to use the SR20 engine from previous generations, its chassis and running gear underwent a comprehensive redesign. With improved body rigidity, upgraded brakes, a more aggressive suspension setup, and the addition of a helical LSD, the S15 delivered a higher level of performance than its predecessors.
car1448.hero: This popular S15 model included side skirts and a rear spoiler.

car145.desc: First unveiled as the Kopen at the 1999 Tokyo Motor Show, this model entered production in 2002 as the Daihatsu Copen, becoming the company’s first fully convertible kei-class car. With a rigid yet lightweight body and a specially tuned suspension, the Copen delivered sharp and responsive handling. It also drew significant attention for being the first kei-car in the world to feature a power-operated retractable hardtop. Its unique charm led to exports to markets such as the UK and Australia.
car145.hero: A kei car with a sports car heart, this little convertible was at home on the racetrack.

car1458.desc: Unveiled in 2008, the sixth-generation Fairlady Z (Z34) was an all-new model, although it retained a strong resemblance to its Z33 predecessor. Built on the same platform as the V36 Skyline Coupé, it featured a lighter chassis paired with a series of performance enhancements. At its core was the VQ37VHR engine, delivering an impressive 331.4 HP. Suspension and braking systems were also finely tuned, underscoring the model’s performance-focused character.
car1458.hero: A shortened wheelbase plus larger engine equals driving fun in this sixth-gen Z car.

car1461.desc: Built between 1988 and 1993, the S13-generation Silvia won over enthusiasts with its nimble handling and well-balanced rear-wheel-drive layout. Among its various trims, the high-performance K’s stood out—powered by a turbocharged DOHC inline-4, the CA18ET—earning a strong reputation for its versatility and performance. Later, the “Dia Selection” was introduced as a more affordable variant.
car1461.hero: This special S13 had many previously optional items now included as standard equipment.

car1466.desc: After a surprise return to competition, the Nissan GT-R made its debut in the 2008 Super GT Championship. In preparation for upcoming regulation changes, the car received a pipe frame chassis and equipped with the same 4.5-liter V-8 previously used in the Z. The XANAVI NISMO demonstrated remarkable pace from the opening round and ultimately secured the drivers’ championship title.
car1466.hero: This very fast GT-R scored wins at Suzuki, Okayama, and Autopolis in the 2008 Super GT.

car1470.desc: The All Japan Grand Touring Championship (JGTC) ran until 2004, after which it evolved into the current Super GT series. Toyota entered the Supra into JGTC competition in 1994. During that era, the series was largely dominated by the Nissan Skyline GT-R; however, in 1997, the Supra finally broke through, capturing the season title with the No. 36 Castrol TOM'S Supra.
car1470.hero: This car brought an end to the GT-R's domination by taking the title in 1997.

car1474.desc: This limited-production supercar, with only 399 units built, was launched in 2002 to commemorate Ferrari’s 55th anniversary. Its sharp-nosed, Formula 1-inspired design was the work of Ken (Kiyoyuki) Okuyama, then a designer at Pininfarina. The car was constructed with extensive use of carbon composites for both the body panels and much of the framework. At its heart was a specially developed 6.0-liter V-12 producing 650.9 HP and 484.6 ft-lb of torque, allowing the car to reach a top speed of more than 217.5 mph.
car1474.hero: Christened with the name of the founder, this car celebrated the company's 55th anniversary and had a limited 399-production run.

car1480.desc: From the debut of the C6 Z06 in 2005, the Chevrolet Corvette began to show not only the styling but also the performance credentials of a true supercar. By 2008, the ZR1 had taken things even further, matching its high-end rivals from Ferrari and Lamborghini in raw performance. Its supercharged 6.2-liter V-8 produced 638.1 HP, and with a curb weight of just 3325 lbs, it posted a Nürburgring lap time faster than that of the Nissan GT-R.
car1480.hero: The 6th-gen Corvette ZR1 set one of the fastest lap times ever for a production car at the Nürburgring.

car1481.desc: First unveiled at the 1971 Geneva Motor Show, the Lamborghini Countach became the prototypical supercar. The first production version, the LP400, launched in 1974 in a limited run of just 150 units. In 1985, Lamborghini introduced the 5000 Quattrovalvole, powered by a 5.2-liter engine producing 448.7 HP. The final version of the Countach was the 25th Anniversary model, released in 1988, with a total production run of 657 units.
car1481.hero: The final model of the Countach, commemorating the 25th anniversary of Lamborghini.

car1484.desc: First unveiled at the 1971 Geneva Motor Show, the Lamborghini Countach became a landmark in supercar history, drawing global attention with its groundbreaking design and performance. Named after a word from the Piedmontese dialect meaning “surprise,” the Countach lived up to its name in every sense. Marcello Gandini’s bold, near-futuristic styling left an indelible mark on the design language of high-performance cars for generations to follow.
car1484.hero: The futuristic styling of this exotic car attracted quite a bit of attention from all around the world.

car1504.desc: The 458 Italia, introduced at the 2009 Frankfurt Motor Show, succeeded the F430. Built on a new aluminum space frame, it housed a 4499 cc V-8 producing 562.1 HP and 398.5 ft-lb of torque. The upgraded Manettino system allowed seamless control of engine, transmission, and suspension settings. With F1-derived aero design, it hit 0–62.1 mph in 3.4 seconds and topped out at 201.9 mph.
car1504.hero: With an astonishing 562.1 HP under the hood, this V8 mid-engine machine took its heritage from the F430.

car1506.desc: Released in 2008, the Lamborghini Gallardo LP 560-4 delivered a 39.4 HP boost over its predecessor. It retained the 4-wheel-drive system but introduced a new 6-speed E-gear transmission, offering gear shifts 40 percent quicker than before. Weight was also trimmed, bringing the body down to 3108 lbs, while top speed rose to 201.9 mph. With its sleek design and elevated performance, it embodied the peak of refined speed.
car1506.hero: No longer a "baby Lambo," this car possessed top-tier performance.

car1507.desc: Unveiled at the 2009 Frankfurt Motor Show, this striking sports car was distinguished by its signature gull-wing doors. Beneath its all-aluminum body was a newly developed 6.3-liter V-8 engine, producing 563.1 HP and 477.4 ft-lb of torque. The 7-speed dual-clutch transmission was integrated with the rear differential, offering five selectable driving modes. Performance was formidable, with a zero-to-62.1 mph acceleration in just 3.8 seconds and a top speed of 197 mph.
car1507.hero: With the SLS AMG, Mercedes-Benz recreates the 300 SL for the modern era.

car1508.desc: This special edition of the Lancer Evolution VI was introduced to celebrate Tommi Mäkinen’s remarkable achievement of four consecutive WRC drivers’ championships. Tailored for tarmac rallies, its ride height was lowered by 0.4 inches, and low-end torque was increased to enhance everyday drivability. Limited to 2,500 units, it featured an exclusive red body color and matching seats, special alloy wheels, and a large-diameter exhaust silencer, making it as distinctive as it was capable.
car1508.hero: Optional body graphics stood out on this rare Tommi Mäkinen Edition Evo.
car1508.nameLong: Mitsubishi Lancer Evolution VI GSR T.M. EDITION Special Color Package '99
car1508.nameShort: Lancer Evolution VI GSR T.M. SCP '99

car1510.desc: This is a version of the NSX that competed in the 2008 Super GT championship. Despite facing disadvantages that season—including running with the previous year’s chassis, weight handicaps, and a restricted air intake—the car remained competitive thanks to significant improvements in both engine performance and aerodynamics. In Round 8 at Autopolis, the EPSON NSX secured a 2nd-place finish.
car1510.hero: The special race NSX brings to mind the bold driving styles of racers Loic Duval and Katsuyuki Hiranaka.

car1516.desc: This Super GT race car competed during the 2008 season. To enhance aerodynamic efficiency, both the front and rear overhangs were extended, and its compact body proved highly effective on high-speed circuits. Although it didn’t claim any outright wins, its consistent performance throughout the season earned enough points to secure the team title.
car1516.hero: Won the Super GT team title with its stable performance on high-speed circuits.

car1523.desc: The car symbolized FIAT’s original mission of delivering accessible, everyday mobility. The first 500, born in 1957, featured an extremely compact body housing a 497 cc engine with just 14.8 HP, mounted at the rear. Despite its modest power, the car offered surprising practicality and affordability, quickly gaining popularity and spawning numerous Abarth-tuned variants. The F model introduced front-hinged doors for the first time.
car1523.hero: Small, versatile and inexpensive, this minimalist car could also be raced.

car1527.desc: Thanks to its affordable pricing and endearing styling, the original FIAT 500 sold more than four million units over its 20-year production run starting in 1957. Half a century after the second-generation model, the third-generation FIAT 500 arrived. Making its debut at the 2004 Geneva Motor Show, the new Fiat 500 launched to widespread acclaim in the summer of 2007. It was affectionately known around the world as the Cinquecento—Italian for “500."
car1527.hero: The Italian version of the people's car makes a comeback after a 50-year hiatus.

car1528.desc: The SLR McLaren was the production realization of the 1999 Mercedes-Benz Vision SLR concept. Its most distinctive feature was the carbon-fiber monocoque chassis, dramatically reducing weight while enhancing rigidity. Power came from a 5.5-liter SOHC V-8 equipped with a twin-screw supercharger, paired with a 5-speed automatic transmission offering sport, comfort, and manual modes.
car1528.hero: The already aggressive-looking SLR McLaren looked even more ominous with optional 19-inch wheels.

car1536.desc: This was a track-only evolution of the Zonda, unveiled in 1999. Its mid-mounted AMG V-12 delivered 739.6 HP and 520.8 ft-lb of torque. To enhance stability, both the wheelbase and track width were extended. The car was capable of reaching a top speed of 217.5 mph and could accelerate from zero to 62.1 mph in just 2.7 seconds.
car1536.hero: The Zonda R featured an adjustable rear wing and a sequential-shift 6-speed transmission.

car1537.desc: The third-generation Prius remained synonymous with hybrid technology. This iteration sought to elevate not only its environmental credentials but also the pleasure of driving itself. Its newly sculpted body featured a sleek, aerodynamic silhouette that conveyed a sense of motion even at rest. The engine was upsized to 1.8 liters, and more than 90 percent of the hybrid system components were newly developed. Fuel efficiency reached an astonishing 89.4 MPG, introducing a new dimension to the driving experience, one where performance met the pure satisfaction of exceptional economy.
car1537.hero: This Prius variant focused on both increased performance and delivering better overall driving pleasure.

car1539.desc: This was the high-performance variant of the GranTurismo, introduced at the 2008 Geneva Motor Show. Its DOHC V-8 engine had its displacement increased to 4.7 liters, while the transmission and rear differential were integrated into a transaxle layout. It also became the first in the series to adopt the two-pedal semi-automatic MC Shift system.
car1539.hero: True to its Italian heritage, this grand tourer was defined by class, performance and elegance.

car1540.desc: The McLaren F1 was a groundbreaking supercar conceived by legendary Formula 1 designer Gordon Murray. From its unique 3-seat configuration, with the driver positioned at the center, to its balanced weight distribution, the F1 introduced a host of innovations that redefined what a road car could be. Celebrated worldwide, it earned acclaim not only as the fastest production car of its time but also for its usability in everyday driving.
car1540.hero: The ultra-exotic McLaren F1 exemplified the genius of its designer, Gordon Murray.

car1541.desc: The TTS was the high-performance variant of the TT series, introduced in 2008. Its powertrain featured a 2.0-liter direct-injection turbocharged engine paired with either a 6-speed manual or a 6-speed S-Tronic transmission. The engine block, pistons, and connecting rods were uniquely developed for the TTS, and the turbocharger was upgraded to handle the increased output. Power was delivered through Audi’s proprietary full-time 4-wheel-drive system, enabling a zero-62.1 mph acceleration time of 5.2 seconds with the S-Tronic model, and 5.4 seconds with the manual.
car1541.hero: A high-performance model, aggressively evolved from the TT.

car1542.desc: The third-generation Corvette made its debut in the fall of 1967. Heavily inspired by Chevrolet’s 1965 show car, the Mako Shark II, it introduced a bold new coupe design, characterized by its curvaceous “coke bottle” silhouette, which instantly turned heads. Initially launched simply as the Corvette, the model brought back the Stingray name in 1969, along with a larger engine that added greater versatility and performance.
car1542.hero: Taking design cues from the Mako Shark II concept, this 3rd-gen Corvette was known for its distinctive character.

car1543.desc: This Dodge sports coupe was introduced in 1970, built on the same E-body chassis as the Plymouth Barracuda. Targeting the booming pony car segment favored by younger drivers, it was offered in both hardtop and convertible variants. The high-performance R/T (Road/Track) trim sat at the top of the range, positioned above the standard inline-6 and V-8 models.
car1543.hero: The top-grade model of the Challenger, which impressed with its performance and bold styling.

car1544.desc: Revealed at the 2007 Frankfurt Motor Show in September, the Ferrari 430 Scuderia reflected the brand’s Formula 1 expertise. Compared to the base F430, it featured enhanced aerodynamics, weight reduction, and more power. The result was a 0–62.1 mph sprint in just 3.6 seconds and a top speed of 198.8 mph.
car1544.hero: A road-going racer that greatly improved upon the performance of the F430.

car1545.desc: A high-performance evolution of Lamborghini’s flagship Murciélago made its debut in 2006. The transversely mounted V-12 engine, originally displacing 6.2 liters, was enlarged to 6.5 liters, delivering an impressive 631.2 HP. Its exterior received a comprehensive aerodynamic redesign, complemented by upgrades to the transmission and electronic systems.
car1545.hero: With 631.2 HP, the flagship supercar from Lamborghini reached a top speed of 211.3 mph.

car1549.desc: The Version NISMO Type 380RS was a fully tuned Z33 Fairlady Z developed by NISMO. Power House Amuse took it a step further, crafting the Amuse NISMO 380RS Super Leggera. The standout upgrade was its weight reduction of 309 lbs, a nod to the Super Leggera name—Italian for "super light."
car1549.hero: Modified by Amuse, this Z car not only looked great, but also underwent a major weight reduction.

car1551.desc: The 330 P4 was Ferrari’s answer to the dominance of the Ford GT. Although only four units were ever made, a berlinetta version for high-speed tracks and a roofless spider for reduced weight were produced. It won its debut race at the 24 Hours of Daytona. While Ford ultimately triumphed at Le Mans, Ferrari secured the World Sportscar Championship title.
car1551.hero: This V12-powered P Series race car was known as "the most beautiful machine ever."

car1553.desc: Completed in 1966, this was Jaguar’s first mid-engine racing sports car. Its low, aerodynamic body—reminiscent of the E-type—housed a 495.1 HP 5.0-liter DOHC V-12. Although it showed great promise as a competitive circuit machine, Jaguar’s management at the time had little interest in motorsport, and the project was ultimately cancelled. Often regarded as Jaguar’s most beautiful race car, it faded into history without ever turning a wheel in competition.
car1553.hero: A dream car that never came to be, this beautiful V12 mid-engine race car disappeared.

car1562.desc: This ultimate sports car aimed to carry forward the spirit and performance legacy of the Toyota 2000GT. Its carbon-fiber body was produced through automated processes, and the transaxle and radiator were mounted at the rear to achieve a near-perfect 48:52 front-to-rear weight distribution. Under the hood was a 4.8-liter V-10 with a 72-degree bank angle. Its distinctive sound was tuned in collaboration with Yamaha. Only 500 units were produced, making it as rare as it was ambitious.
car1562.hero: This ultra high-tech sports car achieved ultimate performance with mass-production quality.

car1563.desc: The Renault Sport Mégane Trophy was developed specifically for the Mégane Trophy race series, which began in 2005. While retaining the overall silhouette of the production Mégane, the Trophy version featured far more aggressive styling and a mid-mounted 355 HP 3.5-liter V-6 in a lightweight 2194 lbs package. A 6-speed two-pedal manual transmission with paddle shifters delivered quick, precise gear changes. The suspension and brakes were full racing spec.
car1563.hero: Aggressive looks topped off by gullwing doors highlight this Mégane Trophy.

car1565.desc: Following this triumph, Ford responded to updated FIA regulations by developing the Mark IV—a new test car with a highly aerodynamic body. This redesign pushed the top speed to 215.6 mph and significantly improved high-speed stability, crucial to its success in the 1967 Le Mans. There, the Mark IV outpaced its rival by five laps, securing a second consecutive victory for Ford at the famed endurance race.
car1565.hero: This race car represented Ford's last effort to challenge for the 24 Hours of Le Mans title.

car1578.desc: The original 8C took its name from the 8-cylinder engine designed by the legendary Vittorio Jano. Beneath its timeless bodywork lay a 4.7-liter V-8, tuned by Alfa Romeo to deliver 443.8 HP. With a top speed of 180.2 mph and a 0–62.1 mph sprint time of under 4.2 seconds, it rivaled—and in some cases surpassed—contemporary supercars. Limited to just 500 units worldwide, the car sold out almost immediately upon its release.
car1578.hero: This car marked Alfa Romeo's return to the rear-drive coupe and possessed a top speed of 180.2 mph plus.

car1581.desc: Based on the GT by Citroën, first shown at the 2008 Paris Motor Show, this model has been reimagined as the ultimate road-going version. The most significant change lay in the powertrain, transformed from a high-performance EV into a V-8-powered, mid-engine sports car. Its distinctive, armor-like styling was preserved, creating a uniquely striking and high-performance machine built for the road.
car1581.hero: From dream to reality, the supercar concept developed by Citroën and Gran Turismo becomes a V8-powered mid-engine sports car.

car1582.desc: Lamborghini’s first supercar, the Miura P400, debuted in 1966 and marked a revolutionary leap in automotive design—catapulting the brand onto the global stage. This groundbreaking machine was the result of a collaboration between industry legends: Marcello Gandini, then chief designer at Bertone; Gian Paolo Dallara, who engineered the chassis; and Paolo Stanzani, who would go on to create the Countach.
car1582.hero: This car put Lamborghini on the supercar map and defined the genre.

car1645.desc: This racing machine was the result of a collaborative effort between Alfa Romeo and Carrozzeria Zagato. Based on the TZ, its body shell was replaced with lightweight FRP, while the nose and roof were lowered to enhance aerodynamic performance. Under the hood, it featured the twin-ignition cylinder head from the Giulia GTA, allowing it to produce 162.7 HP and reach a top speed of 152.2 mph.
car1645.hero: Both in style and substance, this car represented all that was good about sports cars in the 1960s.
car1645.nameLong: Alfa Romeo GIULIA TZ2 carrozzata da ZAGATO '65

car1646.desc: Peugeot developed the 908 HDi FAP to compete at the highest level of prototype racing. During 2007 and 2008, it took part in events such as the Le Mans Series, serving as a platform for ongoing research and development. In 2009, the car finally triumphed over its chief rival—Audi’s diesel-powered R10—securing a dominant 1–2 finish at Le Mans. Although it was unable to repeat the feat in 2010, the 908 HDi FAP continued to deliver commendable results.
car1646.hero: This Peugeot LMP took the top four spots in qualifying for the 2010 24 Hours of Le Mans, but not one finished the race.

car1671.desc: Dr. Ferdinand Porsche’s Volkswagen was developed into a broad range of variants. One such version was the Sambabus, which reimagined the car as a van with generous luggage capacity. By positioning the horizontally-opposed engine at the very rear, designers were able to create a wide, low floor while preserving the vehicle’s compact footprint. This clever layout gave the model a number of advantages as a commercial vehicle, adding to its appeal and versatility.
car1671.hero: With maximum interior space in a small body, this cute bus was highly efficient.

car1689.desc: First introduced in 1972, the Civic is Honda’s longest-running model. In 1997, the first Civic Type R made its debut, based on the sixth-generation Civic. At its heart was the B16B—a 1.6-liter naturally-aspirated inline-4 DOHC engine that delivered an impressive 182.4 HP. This version is an original Gran Turismo-tuned model based on the 1997 Civic Type R (EK).
car1689.hero: The first Type R model tuned by Gran Turismo.
car1689.nameLong: Honda Civic Type R (EK) Touring Car

car1722.desc: Bearing the name MP4—a subtle nod to McLaren’s F1—the MP4-12C stood out for its advanced carbon-composite "MonoCell" chassis. This lightweight structure played a crucial role in reducing overall mass, allowing the car, despite its relatively modest power figures by McLaren standards, to equal or even surpass the performance of its chief rival, the Ferrari 458 Italia.
car1722.hero: The MP4-12C was the first McLaren production car since the McLaren F1 road car.

car1729.desc: Following its debut in 1964, the original Ford Mustang underwent a transformation in 1969, adopting a larger and more muscular body design. Among the updated lineup, the Mach 1, distinguished by its bold SportsRoof fastback, stood out for its aggressive appearance. Its styling left a lasting impression, influencing sports car design across the globe for years to come.
car1729.hero: With more muscle than others in its class, this pony car set a new standard for aggressiveness.

car173.desc: The Renault R5 ("Cinq") Turbo drew major attention when it was introduced at the 1978 Paris Motor Show. Initially developed as a prototype for the World Rally Championship (WRC), a production version followed in 1980. The transformation was dramatic, its front-engine/front-wheel-drive layout replaced with a mid-engine/rear-wheel-drive one. The new engine delivered 1.5 times the power and more than three times the torque compared to the standard model. Making its debut at the 1980 WRC Tour de Corse, the R5 Turbo dominated the field, establishing Renault as a serious WRC force.
car173.hero: The rear-mid-engine layout and ultra-wide rear fenders of this Renault hatchback set the 1980s auto industry on the right track.

car1746.desc: The Eunos Roadster (NA Special Package) '89 has been specially tuned by Gran Turismo to create this original machine. While the engine and suspension have been enhanced and aerodynamic components added, it faithfully preserves the Roadster’s hallmark "Jinba Ittai," the feeling of unity between car and driver. This spartan lightweight can even hold its own in touring car races.
car1746.hero: A first-generation Mazda Roadster, tuned to perfection by Gran Turismo.

car1770.desc: The original Aventador made its debut at the 2011 Geneva Motor Show, taking over from the Murciélago. Its chassis was thoroughly reengineered, now utilizing a carbon monocoque paired with aluminum subframes at both ends, replacing the steel tube frame of its predecessor. Thanks to the extensive use of carbon fiber and aluminum, the SV achieved an impressively low dry weight of just 3472 lbs for a car in this class.
car1770.hero: The new flagship of the heralded supercar company was nothing short of awesome.

car1773.desc: The Scirocco R was a high-performance sports coupe developed from the core architecture of the Golf. Its body sat lower, with a wider track for enhanced stability, and is fitted with unique bumpers, side skirts, and a roof-mounted spoiler. Significant upgrades were made to the suspension and braking systems. Lighter than the Golf R of the same era, the Scirocco R was refined into a nimble, high-spec sports machine with a sharp, responsive edge.
car1773.hero: This attractive coupe possesses the sharp cornering ability of a fully-fledged sports car.

car1778.desc: Often referred to by its nicknames—most famously, the "Beetle"—the Volkswagen Type I was a rear-wheel-drive vehicle powered by an air-cooled, rear-mounted 4-cylinder engine. Produced from 1938 to 2003, it saw over 21 million units built. The Volkswagen 1200 was the official designation for the version produced between the mid-1950s and late 1960s, which featured a 1.2-liter engine.
car1778.hero: Its cute silhouette and rear-engine layout made this car an icon in automobiledom.

car1796.desc: The Alpine A110 was a classic French sports car with a celebrated heritage in rally racing. With its rear-engine layout and lightweight construction, it delivered superb traction and quickly rose to prominence in international rally events, claiming numerous victories. First introduced in 1963 with a 1.1-liter engine, the A110 saw gradual increases in displacement to remain competitive over time. The pinnacle of the lineup was arguably the 1600S, which came equipped with a 1.6-liter engine.
car1796.hero: The swoopy rear-engined Alpine was powered by a Renault engine.

car1797.desc: The SLS AMG GT3 was a race machine based on the road-going SLS AMG. It retained the same fundamental powerplant as the production model. Although official output figures were never released, estimates placed it at over 591.7 HP. Entering full-scale competition in 2011, the car secured 25 victories out of the 101 races it contested that year.
car1797.hero: This race car version of Mercedes-Benz's supercar was tailored to FIA GT3 regulations.

car187.desc: Introduced in 2000 by British sports car manufacturer TVR, this two-door coupe featured a detachable roof and a distinctive exterior design that blended bold curves with aggressive lines. Power came from TVR’s in-house developed 4.0L inline-6, known as the Speed 6, which produced 359 HP. With a lightweight body tipping the scales at just 2425 lbs, the car delivered truly staggering performance.
car187.hero: This unique machine offers a classic sports car feel to enthusiast drivers of today.

car1893.desc: This luxury convertible sports car drew inspiration from the iconic BMW 507 of the 1950s. Its aluminum space frame housed the same 5.0-liter V-8 and 6-speed manual transmission found in the E39 M5, producing 394.5 HP and capable of accelerating from zero to 62.1 mph in just 4.7 seconds. It also earned cinematic fame as the featured Bond car in a 007 movie.
car1893.hero: BMW's contemporary Z8 roadster has the distinction of being one of James Bond's rare non-British vehicles.

car1895.desc: An evolution of the Dino 206GT introduced in 1968, the Dino 246GT was named in honor of Enzo Ferrari’s late son. The aluminum body was replaced with a steel construction, and the wheelbase was extended to enhance control and high-speed stability. The cast-iron block V-6 was enlarged to 2.4 liters, producing 192.3 HP and 166.4 ft-lb of torque.
car1895.hero: This collector's car took the nickname of Enzo Ferrari's son, Alfredo "Dino," who passed away at the age of 24.

car1896.desc: This vehicle marked Tesla’s second production model, following the Roadster. Its spacious sedan form incorporated a rear hatch, classifying it as a 5-door. Buyers could choose from three distinct battery capacities, each aligned with a specific price tier. At the top of the range, the Signature Performance variant delivered 410.3 HP and 441.2 ft-lb of torque, firmly placing it in supercar territory.
car1896.hero: A stylish 5-door sedan introduced by Tesla, the pioneer of electric cars.

car1898.desc: This was Aston Martin’s new flagship model, unveiled in 2009. Although it shared visual cues with the DB9 and DBS, it was, in fact, a bespoke creation developed almost entirely from the ground up. At its heart lay a 7.3-liter V-12 engine, co-developed with Cosworth, producing 749.5 HP and 549.7 ft-lb of torque, making it the most powerful naturally aspirated engine ever fitted to a production car. Initially priced at £1,200,000 in the UK, all 77 units were spoken for within a year of deliveries commencing in early 2011.
car1898.hero: This handsome supercar was limited to 77 units, and could very well be the most desirable British car ever.

car1900.desc: This was a masterpiece roadster crafted by legendary designer Virgil Exner in 1960. Its asymmetrical styling, hood bulge, and dramatic aero fins gave the impression of Exner’s personal interpretation of a 1950s-era race car. It was awarded the Gran Turismo Trophy in 2011.
car1900.hero: The Gran Turismo Trophy winner, with unique asymmetric styling.

car1902.desc: Based on the E89-generation Z4, BMW’s GT3 race machine began competition in 2010. Weight was reduced by 661 lbs through extensive modifications, including the replacement of the retractable roof with a fixed panel. The engine was also changed to a 4.0-liter V-8. In 2011, the car was further refined with wider fenders and a larger 4.4-liter engine producing 507.9 HP. Paired with an upgraded paddle-shift transmission, this Z4 achieved a series of remarkable results in some of the world’s most fiercely contested GT races.
car1902.hero: Starting the 2011 24 Hours of Spa from the 49th position on the grid, this BMW Z4 GT3 crossed the finish line in a remarkable 2nd place.

car1904.desc: The GT version, developed from this high-performance base, was extensively modified for racing. Many body panels were replaced with carbon fiber, cutting weight down to 2745 lbs, while the fenders were flared, widening the body by 4.3 inches. Even with a restrictor in place, the 4.0-liter V-8 still produced an impressive 493.1 HP.
car1904.hero: BMW's M3 GT2 raced in premier endurance contests including the ALMS and ILMC series as well as the 24 Hours of Nürburgring.

car1905.desc: In 2013, Gran Turismo series producer Kazunori Yamauchi partnered with Schulze Motorsport to take on the Nürburgring 24 Hours. The GT-R GT3 was specially prepared for the race, with support from Polyphony Digital’s technical team. Data gathered from the car’s performance was later used to enhance the realism of Gran Turismo’s simulation engine.
car1905.hero: Kazunori Yamauchi and this GT-R NISMO GT3 fought hard in the Nürburgring race in 2013.

car1907.desc: The X-BOW was the first sports car developed by Austrian motorcycle manufacturer KTM. Pronounced “Crossbow,” it drew inspiration from the mechanical bow weapon that shares its name. Stripped of doors and windows, this minimalist two-seater eliminated all superfluous features in pursuit of pure performance. With its precise handling, the car was capable of sustaining up to 1.5 lateral Gs through corners.
car1907.hero: The KTM X-Bow is a unique Audi turbo-powered track car from the Austrian motorcycle manufacturer.

car1916.desc:
The Stingray name returned with the launch of the seventh-generation Corvette. Built using lightweight materials, the car maintained a nearly perfect 50:50 front-to-rear weight distribution, even with its powerful 6.2-liter LT1 V-8, matching the benchmark set by the world’s finest sports cars. 
Equipped with the Z51 performance package, with features such as an electronic LSD, dry sump lubrication, and high-performance brakes, the car was able to accelerate from zero to 60 mph in just 3.8 seconds.
car1916.hero: The seventh-generation Corvette is the first to wear the "Stingray" badge since the 1976 third-generation model.

car1925.desc: This high-performance Mustang was developed by Ford in collaboration with Carroll Shelby to compete in the SCCA, a premier American sports car racing series. The lightened body was equipped with race suspension and an LSD, while at its heart sat the 289 engine, producing 301.8 HP. Beginning in 1965, it went on to dominate the series for three consecutive years.
car1925.hero: This highly collectible Mustang earned a great track record in SCCA racing.

car1926.desc: The AC Cobra had already made a name for itself on the racing scene in the 1960s, and its closed-roof variant was the Shelby Cobra Coupe. While the open-bodied Cobra excelled in acceleration and handling, it lagged behind in top speed due to poor aerodynamics. That changed with a coupe body designed by Pete Brock, which dramatically improved the car’s airflow and added more than 18.6 mph to its top speed. With its full potential unlocked, the Cobra Coupe went on to win numerous races over the following two years.
car1926.hero: Only 6 units of the legendary, and very successful, Shelby Daytona Coupe race car were ever made.

car1927.desc: Audi shook the rallying world in 1981 with the debut of its full-time 4-wheel-drive system in the World Rally Championship. This particular variant, a modified version of the Sport quattro S1, was tailored specifically for hill climb competitions, equipped with radical ground effects that pushed the limits of aerodynamics. In 1987, Walter Röhrl piloted this machine to a record-breaking triumph at the Pikes Peak International Hill Climb.
car1927.hero: The 1987 winner of the Pikes Peak that also set a new record that year.
car1927.nameLong: Audi Sport quattro S1 Pikes Peak '87

car1931.desc: Ferrari shortened the wheelbase of the 250 GT Berlinetta for sharper track handling. That change bore fruit with numerous race victories starting in 1960, including wins at the Tour de France and Nürburgring 621.4 miles. Just 162 units were built before its successor, the iconic 250 GTO, took over in 1962.
car1931.hero: A predecessor to the 250 GTO, this car racked up numerous wins in the world of endurance racing.

car1932.desc: Another Maserati highlight, an aerodynamic test vehicle, was unveiled at the 1952 Turin Motor Show. Based on a FIAT platform, the car showcased strikingly original styling by Franco Scaglione and was powered by a 1.5-liter engine tuned by Abarth to deliver 73 HP. The only example ever built was later shown at the Pebble Beach Concours d’Elegance in recent years, where it earned the prestigious Gran Turismo trophy.
car1932.hero: A futuristic-looking design featuring a large central headlight, this Abarth was first shown at the 1952 Turin Motor Show.

car1933.desc: This 3-door hatchback was released in the B-segment as a replacement for Alfa Romeo’s previous entry-level model, the 147. Its name was inspired by Milan and Torino—two cities central to Alfa Romeo’s history. The standard powerplant was a turbocharged 1.4-liter DOHC, with the 1.4 Sport variant producing 152.9 HP and 166.4 ft-lb of torque, paired with a 6-speed manual transmission. With a top speed of 133.6 mph and a zero-62.1 mph time of 8.0 seconds, it delivered more than respectable performance for its class.
car1933.hero: Alfa Romeo's MiTo hatchback brings a dash of Italian flair to the compact car segment.

car1935.desc: In a bold move to leave its mark on the racing world, Ford partnered with Lola Cars to develop the Mark I, which was completed in 1964. Based on the Lola-designed Mk6, the car was introduced as the Ford GT. The name "GT40" was coined by a reporter, amazed by the car’s height—just 40 inches from the ground. At the 1966 24 Hours of Le Mans, the improved Mark II version achieved a legendary 1-2-3 finish.
car1935.hero: This historic machine achieved a much-desired Le Mans victory with an incredible 1-2-3 finish.

car1956.desc: The third-generation Viper made its debut in 2012. A key highlight of this new model was that it was released under SRT, Chrysler’s high-performance brand. Although the V-10 engine retained its 8.4-liter displacement, numerous internal upgrades boosted output to 640 HP and 600.3 ft-lb of torque. As with previous generations, the chassis featured a steel tube frame, though torsional rigidity was improved by 50 percent. At the top of the range, the GTS offered an active suspension system.
car1956.hero: This third-generation Viper is now marketed under Dodge's extreme performance SRT brand.

car1965.desc: This prototype race car was developed by Audi. While it shared lineage with the diesel-powered R10 and R15, the R18 was Audi’s first closed-cockpit design since the R8C of 1999. Its engine produced a modest 532.5 HP—less than its recent predecessors—but compensated with aggressive weight reduction and the aerodynamic efficiency afforded by its enclosed bodywork. In 2011, the R18 claimed overall victory at Le Mans.
car1965.hero: This diesel-powered R18 TDI scored yet another victory for Audi at the 24 Hours of Le Mans in 2011.

car1973.desc: This was a factory-tuned version of the FIAT 500, developed by the iconic Italian performance brand Abarth, which returned to the scene in 2007. Powered by a turbocharged 1.4-liter DOHC engine delivering 133.1 HP and 151.9 ft-lb of torque. Tipping the scales at just 2447 lbs, the car accelerated from zero to 62.1 mph in 7.9 seconds and reached a top speed of 127.4 mph. The design carried the unmistakable presence of an Abarth, with aggressive bumpers, flared side skirts, and a roof-mounted spoiler.
car1973.hero: The Abarth returned yet again with bolder looks and performance, this time in the form of the timeless "500."

car1975.desc: This concept car was created to celebrate the 50th anniversary of Mazda’s founding. Its bullet-shaped body was mounted on a steel tube space frame and powered by a 10A-type rotary engine originally developed for the 24 Hours of Spa, delivering around 246.5 HP. Although it appeared publicly in three different body colors, later investigation revealed it was, in fact, a single car repainted for each appearance.
car1975.hero: This ultra-exotic concept featured a rotary engine and cutting-edge technology.

car1984.desc: This race version was based on McLaren’s first full-scale road car, the F1. At the rain-soaked 1995 24 Hours of Le Mans, the F1 GTR defied the odds, outperforming purpose-built prototype racers to claim overall victory. Car No. 59, backed by the factory and driven by Yannick Dalmas, Masanori Sekiya, and JJ Lehto, etched its name into motorsports history.
car1984.hero: The ultimate automobile by McLaren would go on to win both the BPR series and the 24 Hours of Le Mans.

car1985.desc: This was a quintessential example of a 1970s American muscle car. The bold firebird decal emblazoned across the hood became a cultural icon, especially popular among younger enthusiasts of the era. Although it shared its underpinnings with the Chevrolet Camaro, the top-tier Trans Am distinguished itself with an exclusive 6.6-liter engine, not offered on its Chevrolet sibling, making it the pride of Pontiac.
car1985.hero: Made famous by Burt Reynolds in "Smokey and the Bandit," this was one of the leading '70s muscle cars.

car1986.desc: This high-performance version of the Renault 8 was tuned by Amédée Gordini, known as "The Sorcerer" for his remarkable engine tuning. Building on the strengths of the original 1108 cc compact sedan, Gordini transformed the modest Renault 8 into a formidable touring machine, blending precision engineering with motorsport spirit. In 1966, the engine was enlarged to 1300 cc and paired with a 5-speed transmission, further unlocking its performance potential. With its distinctive character and motorsport pedigree, this automotive gem holds a cherished place in the hearts of enthusiasts to this day.
car1986.hero: A French icon of the '60s, the R8 Gordini is still popular half a century after its birth.

car1987.desc: Based on the third-generation Mégane 3-door coupe, the Mégane R.S. was factory-tuned by Renault Sport for high performance. With bespoke ground effects and a newly developed chassis, it delivered exceptional cornering capability—earning its reputation as one of the fastest front-wheel-drive cars of its time. In 2011, the Mégane R.S. Trophy was introduced. With just 500 units produced worldwide, it made headlines by setting a new Nürburgring lap record for mass-produced front-wheel-drive cars, clocking in at 8 minutes and 7.97 seconds.
car1987.hero: This limited-edition Renault set a lap record at the Nürburgring.

car1990.desc: Based on the Diablo GT2—a full race car built for FIA GT championships—the Diablo GT was a street-legal version that had been detuned and modified for road use. Its 6.0-liter V-12 engine produced 567.1 HP and 462.9 ft-lb of torque. Weighing in at just 3285 lbs—88 lbs lighter than the Diablo SV—the GT was capable of reaching an astonishing top speed of 210 mph.
car1990.hero: The 80-car limited-edition model that was positioned as "The Ultimate Diablo."

car201.desc: This automotive masterpiece marked the revival of the lightweight sports car as the 20th century drew to a close. First introduced in 1989 with a 1.6-liter engine, the model saw its displacement increased to 1.8 liters in 1993. Its true appeal lay in its mechanical purity—the transmission and rear differential were unified by an aluminum powerplant frame, while double wishbone suspension and disc brakes at all four corners delivered precise, responsive handling.
car201.hero: Mazda's Eunos Roadster is credited with reviving the small fun-to-drive rear-drive convertible sports car.

car2010.desc: Back then, the line between road and race cars was thin, and the 250 GT Berlinetta embodied both worlds. The "GTO" name marked its homologation for GT racing. A tubular steel chassis supported the aluminum bodywork, optimizing both weight and rigidity. Its 3.0-liter V-12, fed by six carburetors, produced 295.9 HP. The right-hand-drive model developed for the UK performed admirably, often finishing on the podium.
car2010.hero: This ultra-popular car was built to win the GT Class International Championship title.

car2011.desc: The 500 Mondial Pinin Farina Coupe, a car built for the 1954 Tour de France, featured a chassis and engine developed by Ferrari and bodywork by Pininfarina. Although it never competed in the Tour as intended, an unrestored example later won the prestigious Gran Turismo Award at the 2012 Pebble Beach Concours d’Elegance.
car2011.hero: A priceless unrestored example of a Gran Turismo Award winner.

car2017.desc: To qualify for Group B, Ferrari built 200 examples of this homologation special. Although it looked like the 308, it featured a longer wheelbase by 4.3 inches and a longitudinally mounted engine, making it mechanically distinct. The twin-turbocharged 2.8-liter V-8 delivered 394.5 HP, making it the fastest road-going Ferrari at the time.
car2017.hero: At first glance, this monster car appears to be an offshoot model, but it's 100% custom-built on the inside, and produces over 394 horsepower.

car2018.desc: The 365 GTB/4—aka Daytona—was the last Ferrari to have a front-mounted V-12 and made its debut at the 1968 Paris Motor Show. It wore sleek bodywork penned by Leonardo Fioravanti, with a 4390 cc DOHC V-12 powerplant residing underneath. With a top speed of 174 mph, it matched the Lamborghini Miura as the fastest production car of its time.
car2018.hero: The ultimate super sport, this front engine, rear-wheel drive machine rivaled the Miura for the highest top speed of its day.

car2026.desc: After making hybrids mainstream with the Prius, Toyota introduced the Aqua, a smaller, more fuel-efficient hybrid. Its hybrid system was a lighter, optimized version of that used in the third-generation Prius. In JC08 fuel economy tests conducted in Japan, it reached a maximum efficiency of 83.3 MPG. Internationally, the car was marketed as the Prius C.
car2026.hero: More economical than the larger Prius, this model is helping to expand the hybrid vehicle market.

car203.desc: This car introduced the concept of the Type R, a road-going race car. At its heart was the 1.8-liter VTEC B18C engine, hand-built with a high-compression head and carefully matched connecting rods to produce 197.2 HP. While performance parts like the helical LSD added weight, it was offset by stripping out comfort features, resulting in pure speed.
car203.hero: This third-gen Integra Type R received more power and hand-crafted tuning.

car204.desc: In Honda’s lineup, the "Type R" designation signified production models specifically tuned for high performance. The Civic Type R first appeared in August 1997. Based on the sixth-generation EK Civic, it was powered by the B16B 1.6-liter inline-4 DOHC 16-valve engine. Thanks to Honda’s VTEC system, it produced 182.4 HP at 8200 rpm without any forced induction. The model quickly earned a reputation in motorsports, becoming a favorite among amateur racers.
car204.hero: This car represented the first Type R model that eventually dominated circuits around the world.

car2049.desc: This car was the ultimate expression of a modern super sports machine. First unveiled at the 2005 Tokyo Motor Show, it delivered figures rarely seen even among elite supercars: 987.2 HP, a top speed of 252.9 mph, and a price tag of one million euros. Its engine was an 8.0-liter W-16 equipped with four turbochargers, paired with a 7-speed DSG transmission. To access its maximum velocity, a special key was required to activate top-speed mode, allowing the car to exceed 233 mph.
car2049.hero: With a little help from a special key, this remarkable automobile reached speeds of over 233 mph.

car205.desc: The FD3S, the third generation of the RX-7, was introduced in December 1991. Its widened body accommodated broader tires for improved grip, while extensive use of aluminum components throughout the chassis brought the weight down to just under 2646 lbs. Although it retained the 13B engine from the FC3S, the FD3S introduced a sequential twin-turbo system, boosting output to 251.5 HP and 217.0 ft-lb of torque. The lightest variant, the Type S, achieved a power-to-weight ratio of 4.97 kg/HP, making it the most potent RX-7 ever produced.
car205.hero: This final version of the Mazda RX-7 marked the end of an excellent 25-year run for the model.
car205.nameLong: Mazda RX-7 Spirit R Type A (FD) '02

car2050.desc: Pagani introduced the Huayra in 2011 as the successor to the Zonda. Its monocoque chassis combined carbon fiber and titanium, delivering both exceptional strength and lightness, while gullwing doors added to its striking design. Powered by an AMG-built twin-turbo 6.0-liter V-12 paired with a 7-speed sequential transmission, the Huayra could accelerate from zero to 62.1 mph in just 3.2 seconds and reach a top speed of 234.9 mph.
car2050.hero: A car with bold styling, a lavish interior and a 6.0-liter twin-turbo Mercedes-AMG V12.

car2051.desc: This sports coupe used the same platform as the Genesis luxury sedan. It was 13.6 inches shorter overall, with a wheelbase 4.5 inches shorter. Combined with a front-engine/rear-wheel-drive layout and 4-wheel independent suspension, the car possessed sharp handling dynamics. In 2012, the model received updates that increased engine output. With its 3.8-liter V-6 producing around 345.2 HP, it achieved performance approaching supercar territory.
car2051.hero: Circuit-developed components characterized this high-performance sports car.

car2055.desc: This vehicle marked the launch of the "Vision Gran Turismo" project. Its elegant silhouette was inspired by a feline on the hunt, and it featured a hybrid structure of an aluminum space frame and carbon fiber. At just 2994 lbs, it remained relatively lightweight and was powered by an AMG twin-turbo 5.0-liter V-8 producing 430kW (576.9 HP) and 800Nm (590.2 ft-lb) of torque. Specialists also tuned the engine sound, making this machine as thrilling to hear as it was to behold.
car2055.hero: The start of something very special: The very first "Vision Gran Turismo."

car2059.desc: The original Chevrolet Corvette earned numerous race victories. The Corvette SS, a purpose-built race car developed under the direction of GM engineer Zora Arkus-Duntov, featured a 364.9 HP fuel-injected 283 cubic inch engine, and was capable of reaching a top speed of 181.4 mph. However, following a major incident in NASCAR, the AMA imposed a ban on factory-backed race programs. The Stingray Racer was introduced as the successor to the Corvette SS and went on to win the SCCA Class C Modified title in 1959 and 1960.
car2059.hero: The '59 concept embodied a styling that swept the world and remains a part of Corvette history.

car2060.desc: While racing karts are typically viewed as the gateway to motorsports, the Shifter Kart is more akin to a sub-formula race car. Equipped with a 125 cc water-cooled two-stroke engine mated to a 6-speed gearbox and featuring front-only braking, it is capable of reaching speeds up to 124.3 mph. This is a racing machine that hones the skills of race drivers.
car2060.hero: With its tremendous performance and 6-speed gearbox, this kart proves fast enough for full-size tracks.

car207.desc: Introduced in 1989, the second-generation MR2, designated SW20, succeeded the AW11, Japan’s first mass-produced mid-engine sports car. Its body dimensions were stretched to the upper limits of Japan’s Class 5 vehicle regulations, while its design adopted smoother, more aerodynamic lines to emphasize its mid-engine configuration. At launch, the car faced criticism for its challenging handling character, but subsequent refinements transformed it into a well-balanced performer.
car207.hero: The turbocharged model of Toyota's mid-engine sports car featured a rigid chassis that matched its extra power.

car2074.desc: The 3 Series coupe and cabriolet models were split off to form the new 4 Series lineup, with this car serving as the flagship. While its sleek 2-door coupe proportions made it visually striking, its true emphasis was on performance. Under the hood was a twin-turbocharged inline-6 producing 425 HP and 405.8 ft-lb of torque. Paired with an active M differential, adaptive M suspension, and M-specific DSC, it delivered a driving experience worthy of the M badge.
car2074.hero: The BMW M4 becomes the 2-door version of the daunting M3.

car2076.desc: This is a racing version of the Mercedes-Benz AMG Vision Gran Turismo. All interior comforts were removed to bring the weight down to 2866 lbs, while a large fixed rear wing increases downforce for circuit use. The AMG twin-turbo 5.5-liter V-8 has been tuned to produce 591.7 HP. The transmission has been upgraded from the 7-speed dual-clutch to a full sequential system for optimal performance on the track.
car2076.hero: Another "Mercedes-Benz AMG Vision Gran Turismo" ready for competitive racing.
car2076.nameLong: Mercedes-Benz AMG Vision Gran Turismo Racing Series

car2077.desc: The X2014 Series was the result of a collaborative “fan car” project between Red Bull Racing and Gran Turismo. The mid-tier X2014 Standard followed as a more advanced model, developed as a conventional Venturi car. Its design minimized aerodynamic drag through front and rear wheel covers and a glass canopy, while simultaneously increasing downforce.
car2077.hero: A traditional venturi car with the axial flow fan and skirts removed from the X2014.
car2077.nameLong: Gran Turismo Red Bull X2014 Standard

car2078.desc: The X2014 Series was the result of a collaborative “fan car” project between Red Bull Racing and Gran Turismo. The entry-level X2014 Junior model combined a compact body with a similarly compact engine producing approximately 246.5 HP, making it the ideal platform for learning the fundamentals of formula driving.
car2078.hero: A beginner level machine for learning the basics of formula cars.
car2078.nameLong: Gran Turismo Red Bull X2014 Junior

car2080.desc: The Toyota FT-1 is a concept car created by CALTY Design, Toyota’s North American design studio, offering a glimpse into the potential future of the brand’s sports car philosophy. Its projected dimensions are: overall length, 184.1 inches; width 77.6 inches; height 48.2 inches; with a wheelbase of 107.9 inches. The design draws inspiration from Toyota’s rich sports car heritage, beginning with the iconic Toyota 2000GT.
car2080.hero: Toyota's sports design concept presented at the January 2014 Detroit Auto Show.

car2087.desc: This modern road racer was developed by BMW’s design team. Its exterior was sculpted to convey a striking sense of speed, even at a standstill. Power came from a 3.0-liter inline-6 delivering 404kW and 680Nm of torque (541.4 HP/499.1 ft-lb). Remarkably lightweight at just 2601 lbs, the car also achieved ideal 50:50 front-to-rear weight distribution. This Vision Gran Turismo represents a striking blend of BMW’s racing heritage and advanced technology.
car2087.hero: The ultimate road racer that draws its heritage from the glorious touring cars of the '70s.

car2095.desc: This Vision Gran Turismo was created by Mitsubishi Motors, a brand with a strong legacy in events like the Dakar Rally and World Rally Championship (WRC). Inspired by the Mitsubishi Concept XR-PHEV shown at the 2013 Tokyo Motor Show, the concept evolved into a purpose-built racing machine. As a plug-in hybrid EV, it combines electric motors with a conventional engine, delivering massive power to all four wheels through the advanced S-AWC vehicle dynamics control system.
car2095.hero: A hybrid concept packed with know-how and spirit gained through motorsports.
car2095.nameLong: Mitsubishi Concept XR-PHEV EVOLUTION Vision Gran Turismo

car2098.desc: The GTI Roadster Vision Gran Turismo is a supercar that embodies the spirit and performance heritage of Volkswagen’s GTI lineage. At its heart beats a twin-turbocharged 3.0-liter VR6 TSI engine, delivering 502 HP and 484.6 ft-lb of torque. Power is routed through a 7-speed dual-clutch transmission to all four wheels, ensuring exceptional traction and rapid acceleration.
car2098.hero: This supercar with the GTI's DNA possesses race car-like acceleration.
car2098.nameLong: Volkswagen GTI Roadster Vision Gran Turismo

car2099.desc: The SUBARU VIZIV GT Vision Gran Turismo is Subaru’s ultimate expression of a next-generation sports car, carrying forward the brand’s “VIZIV” philosophy—Vision for Innovation. Carbon materials have been used extensively throughout the body, keeping weight down to 3042 lbs. At its heart is a specially tuned horizontally-opposed 2.0-liter engine paired with high-output electric motors, delivering a combined output of 591.7 HP and a peak torque of 800Nm (593.1 ft-lb).
car2099.hero: Subaru's most aggressive sports car ever is potent yet civilized.
car2099.nameLong: SUBARU VIZIV GT Vision Gran Turismo

car210.desc: The R34 GT-R was unveiled in January 1999. In contrast to the larger R33, the new model adopted a more compact, muscular profile—3.0 inches shorter in overall length with a wheelbase reduced by 2.2 inches. The now fully matured RB26DETT engine received a final round of enhancements, pushing torque to 289.3 ft-lb, while refinements to the chassis brought sharper control and more intuitive handling. Crowning the lineup was the limited-edition Nür, fitted with the N1-spec RB26DETT engine, marking the final evolution of the powerplant.
car210.hero: A limited-edition model signifying the end of production, the "Nür" stands for Nürburgring, where the car was developed.
car210.nameLong: Nissan Skyline GT-R V･spec II Nür (R34) '02

car2101.desc: The TS030 Hybrid was developed to compete in the 2012 World Endurance Championship. Its THS-R powertrain was the result of a collaborative effort between Toyota’s production hybrid engineers and the motorsports division at the Higashi-Fuji Technical Center, built around a newly designed V-8 engine. Although it was forced to retire during its debut at the 24 Hours of Le Mans, the car went on to claim three victories over the season, ultimately securing 2nd place in the championship standings.
car2101.hero: The revolutionary hybrid-powered racing prototype that waged war at Le Mans and the WEC.

car2103.desc: The Vision Gran Turismo model was conceived by Marek Reichman’s design team at Aston Martin. It was developed using the same processes as Aston Martin’s production models, at the company’s Gaydon facility in Warwickshire. Power came from a twin-turbo V-12 producing 800 BHP (799.8 HP). The DP-100 also functioned as a testbed for Aston Martin’s future design language and advanced technologies.
car2103.hero: A glimpse of the ultimate British sports car of the future.
car2103.nameLong: Aston Martin DP-100 Vision Gran Turismo

car2106.desc: The FT-1 Vision Gran Turismo itself was a racing adaptation of Toyota’s FT-1 sports design concept, developed by CALTY Design Research, the company’s North American design studio. The design drew heavily from data and practical experience, featuring oversized fenders, an expanded front air intake, a large rear wing, and aggressive front canards.
car2106.hero: The FT-1 design concept transformed into a pure race car.

car2107.desc: Chaparral is a legendary name in motorsport, known for producing unique race cars, and the 2X is unlike anything that came before it. The driver is enclosed within a carbon fiber body, positioned headfirst in a prone posture, as if hovering just centimeters above the track. Power comes from a radical laser pulse propulsion system, which generates thrust and downforce through the rapid expansion of air.
car2107.hero: Experience rocket-like speed produced by laser pulse shock waves!

car2108.desc: This was a car of the future, blending uncompromising, unrestrained performance with a striking, futuristic design. A mid-engine, 4-wheel-drive single-seater, its body was crafted from cutting-edge composite materials. The engine was a 6.98-liter V-10 producing 1,000 horsepower, supported by a pneumatic sub-system. The "X" was the ultimate expression reserved only for drivers deemed capable of handling its 2465.5 HP total output.
car2108.hero: Power exceeding 2500 horsepower and with unrivaled handling, this machine belongs in the hands of only a chosen few.
car2108.nameLong: Dodge SRT Tomahawk X Vision Gran Turismo

car2109.desc: This Vision Gran Turismo represents a MINI built purely for racing. Weighing just 2315 lbs and producing 389.5 HP, it launches from zero to 62.1 mph in a mere 3.5 seconds. Power is sent to all four wheels. Its low-slung silhouette—with the wheels pushed to the very edges—delivers the signature go-kart-like handling MINIs are known for. The result is an exhilarating, track-ready driving experience.
car2109.hero: A race spec Clubman able to reach 0-62.1 mph in just 3.5 seconds, with a top speed of 180.2 mph.

car211.desc: The fifth-generation Lancer Evolution was introduced in January 1998. Developed with the World Rally Championship in mind, the body was widened and the 4G63 engine received further tuning to boost torque. The AYC system (Active Yaw Control) from the Evolution IV was retained, while new inverted dampers and a front helical LSD were added to further elevate performance and cornering ability.
car211.hero: The 5th-gen Evo impressed with its bolder-looking flared fenders and an engine that produced more torque.

car2110.desc: This was a car of the future, blending uncompromising, unrestrained performance with a striking, futuristic design. This mid-engine, all-wheel-drive single-seater featured a body constructed from advanced composite materials. The engine was a 6.98-liter V-10 producing 1,000 horsepower, supported by a pneumatic sub-system. The GTS-R was the dedicated racing variant of the Tomahawk. Drivers were equipped with a specialized racing suit designed to cope with the extraordinary G-forces this machine can generate.
car2110.hero: A lightweight racing version of the visionary near-future single-seater concept.
car2110.nameLong: Dodge SRT Tomahawk GTS-R Vision Gran Turismo

car2111.desc: This was a car of the future, blending uncompromising, unrestrained performance with a striking, futuristic design. A mid-engine, 4-wheel-drive single-seater, its body was crafted from cutting-edge composite materials. The engine was a 6.98-liter V-10 producing 1,000 horsepower, supported by a pneumatic sub-system. The "S" variant represented a more grounded interpretation of the Tomahawk, designed with considerations for open-road drivability. However, unlocking its full potential demanded near-superhuman reflexes from the driver.
car2111.hero: Featuring more than 1000 horsepower from a V-10 and compressed air unit with near-future technology.
car2111.nameLong: Dodge SRT Tomahawk S Vision Gran Turismo

car2112.desc: This was a single-seater sports car created by the renowned French marque Alpine, developed specifically for Gran Turismo players. Its styling followed Alpine’s core philosophy of “speed and excitement, embodied in style,” while paying tribute to the brand’s storied past. This groundbreaking machine bridged the divide between road and track, and between the digital world and physical reality.
car2112.hero: A legendary brand's glimpse of the ultimate future sports car.

car2113.desc: The PEUGEOT Vision Gran Turismo is the result of a collaboration between Peugeot’s design team and the engineers at Peugeot Sport. With a height of just 3.3 ft, its low-slung body hugs the ground. Powered by a turbocharged 3.2-liter V-6 producing 875 ch (874.8 HP), it's clear this machine was conceived to deliver the quintessential driving experience.
car2113.hero: Experience pure steering response in a car that generates powerful downforces directly from its body panels.

car2116.desc: This was a single-seater sports car developed by the celebrated French brand Alpine, crafted specifically for Gran Turismo players. Its styling followed Alpine’s core philosophy of “speed and excitement, embodied in style,” while paying tribute to the brand’s storied past. This groundbreaking machine bridged the divide between road and track, and between the digital world and physical reality.
car2116.hero: A legendary brand's glimpse of the ultimate future sports car.
car2116.nameLong: Alpine Vision Gran Turismo Race Mode

car2117.desc: The INFINITI CONCEPT Vision Gran Turismo was developed by the Infiniti premium brand under the guiding philosophy of “designing a pure INFINITI GT car.” The design team set out to create a full-fledged race machine, while also crafting a seductive and distinctive race design language.
car2117.hero: High performance made possible with a V8 engine and electrical motor. A GT machine packed with the motorsport passion of Asia.

car2118.desc: The Mazda LM55 Vision Gran Turismo was crafted as Mazda’s futuristic vision of endurance racing excellence, with its sights set on total victory at the 24 Hours of Le Mans. Its striking silhouette was shaped by Mazda’s KODO design philosophy, and the front grille echoes the modern face of Mazda’s production lineup with a bold reinterpretation.
car2118.hero: A fusion of speed and elegance, born from the spirit of an unrelenting challenger.

car2119.desc: This Vision Gran Turismo came from a renowned Italian design house.
