car3345.desc: The 2017 GT-R NISMO featured a host of refinements throughout the car. While retaining its bonded body construction and engine specifications, the front window frame was reinforced to improve chassis rigidity. Comfort was also enhanced, making it more livable in urban settings while remaining sharp on the circuit. Aerodynamics saw notable improvements as well, and thanks to a comprehensive redesign, the body generated increased downforce at high speeds, further enhancing performance.
car3345.hero: The 2017 GT-R was a smoother, more refined version of the previous model.

car3346.desc: This is a wild Mustang build crafted by one of Oregon’s most respected custom shops. Everything from the rear seats to the trunk was stripped out to make room for a mid-mounted supercharged 5.4-liter V-8 from a Ford GT—an engine capable of producing up to 850.1 HP. Unveiled at SEMA 2012, the car took home the prestigious GT Award.
car3346.hero: This Mustang, a 2012 GT Award Winner, possessed the heart of a Ford GT.

car3348.desc: The NSX CONCEPT-GT was a purpose-built racing machine developed by Honda, based on the 2012 next-generation NSX concept, to compete in the GT500 class of the Super GT series. At its debut, the car featured a hybrid powertrain, however, by the 2016 season, the hybrid system was removed due to supply challenges from the battery manufacturer. It concluded the season with a 12th-place finish overall.
car3348.hero: This race machine claimed the Super GT championship in 2016 equipped with a conventional gasoline engine.

car3349.desc: The Lexus RC F competed in the Super GT GT500 class from 2014 to 2016. New regulations introduced that year required the monocoque and key components to be shared with DTM counterparts. It ran the same turbocharged 2.0-liter inline-4 used in Super Formula competition. In 2016, the au TOM’S RC F scored points throughout the season, including a 2nd place finish in Round 6, ultimately placing 5th overall in the standings.
car3349.hero: This Toyota/Lexus race car competed under joint regulations between the Super GT Series and DTM.

car3350.desc: The new regulations for 2014 required the GT500 car to share the same monocoque weight and key components with its DTM counterpart. As a result, the GT-R underwent significant revisions to meet GT500 specifications, with ongoing refinements continuing through to the 2016 model. During the 2014 and 2015 seasons, the MOTUL AUTECH GT-R secured back-to-back series championships. Aiming for a third consecutive title in 2016, the team ultimately concluded the season in third place overall.
car3350.hero: This 2016 Super GT race car was driven by the team of Tsugio Matsuda and Ronnie Quintarelli.

car3351.desc: Audi Design created an all-electric Vision Gran Turismo concept. Throughout its body, design cues from the legendary 90 IMSA GTO are prominently featured. The vehicle employed a 4-wheel-drive layout powered by three electric motors—one at the front and two at the rear—delivering a total system output of 600kW (803.7 HP). Audi Sport developed a fully functional e-tron prototype, which went on to demonstrate its formidable performance at tracks worldwide.
car3351.hero: This Vision Gran Turismo is a thrilling embodiment of Audi's electric mobility initiative.

car3352.desc: The GR Supra Racing Concept reimagined the Supra as a race car, appearing 16 years after the model's production ceased in 2002. Its compact two-door coupe body, with classic long-nose, short-deck proportions, utilized cutting-edge materials and engineering to deliver outstanding aerodynamics and handling.
car3352.hero: First seen at the 2018 Geneva Motor Show, this race Supra represented a preview of the production model.

car3353.desc: The Clio R.S. 220 EDC Trophy is a high-performance variant of the fourth-generation Clio, developed by Renault Sport. The 2016 model, known as the R.S. Vision, introduced a distinctive new front bumper design inspired by the pattern of a checkered flag. It also featured updated LED headlights and taillights, along with various other design enhancements throughout.
car3353.hero: This Clio sports model, tuned by Renault Sport, excelled on the race track.
car3353.nameLong: Renault Sport Clio R.S. 220 EDC Trophy '16

car3354.desc: The Toyota 86 and Subaru BRZ sports cars were developed through a collaborative effort between Toyota and Subaru. "BRZ" stood for "Boxer engine, Rear-wheel drive, Zenith." The car was powered by a Subaru 2.0-liter boxer engine paired with Toyota’s D-4S direct injection system. Following its 2012 debut, the car received near-annual updates. The 2015 model notably improved both handling and ride comfort.
car3354.hero: Subaru's first FR sports car featured a boxer engine, giving it a low center of gravity and excellent handling.

car3356.desc: To fully exploit the MINI’s outstanding handling characteristics, the British Motor Corporation joined forces with F1 constructor John Cooper to develop this high-performance variant. The 970 S emerged as a special version, its engine displacement reduced to 970 cc to comply with specific racing class regulations. Whereas the standard 848 cc engine delivered 33.5 HP, this tuned iteration generated an impressive 65.1 HP. Despite a limited production run of just 963 units, the car achieved remarkable success in touring car competitions.
car3356.hero: Devised by Formula 1 legend John Cooper, this very special Mini was intended to excel on the race track.

car3357.desc: The S660 marked Honda’s return to the convertible ultralight kei-sports-car segment 19 years after the end of production of the Beat in 1996. Its all-new body design delivered exceptional rigidity while maintaining a featherweight curb mass in the low 1764 lbs range. Adding to its dynamic prowess, the S660 featured a torque vectoring system that enabled cornering performance previously unimaginable for a kei-car, offering neutral, engaging handling.
car3357.hero: The spiritual successor to the Beat was this small-yet-unadulterated mid-engine kei sports car.

car3358.desc: The 996-generation Porsche 911, introduced in 1997, was the first to feature a GT3 variant. Using the rigid Carrera 4 chassis as a foundation, it incorporated race-grade upgrades to the suspension and brakes, while the engine took on a GT1-spec crankcase for high-rev performance. A total of 1,889 units were produced.
car3358.hero: The 911's first GT3 spec model was introduced for the Type 996. It proved to be very popular, selling 1889 units.

car3359.desc: In 2006, Porsche introduced the GT3 variant for the Type 997. As with its predecessor, it used the Carrera 4 platform, along with upgraded suspension and braking systems. The engine, originally a 3.6-liter unit, was enlarged to 3.8 liters in 2008, increasing output to 428 HP. Electronically controlled PASM dampers were included as standard equipment.
car3359.hero: Featuring adjustable dampers as standard equipment, this GT3 version of the Type 997 made its debut in 2006.

car3360.desc: This circuit-only version of the McLaren P1 was created to commemorate the 20th anniversary of the F1 GTR and its race career throughout the 1990s. The hybrid powertrain, combining electric motors with a twin-turbo V-8, was tuned to produce 986.2 HP. To further enhance its track performance, the car received extensive aerodynamic upgrades, including a prominent rear wing.
car3360.hero: This track-only model further defines the potential of the P1 hybrid supercar.

car3361.desc: A 2-seater sports car released in 1961. Its refined stylings had a profound impact on sports car design all over the world. The 3.6L inline-6 DOHC engine produces 265.3 HP, propelling the lightweight 2687 lbs body to speeds of up to 130.5 mph. 7820 Series I models were produced, with most of them carried over to the United States.
car3361.hero: The masterpiece 2-seater sports car continues to inspire car designers around the world.

car3362.desc: This special model was created to commemorate the 50th anniversary of Ferrari’s founding. Developed under the concept of a “road-going F1 car,” it featured an engine derived from the V-12 in Ferrari’s 1990 "641" F1 machine, enlarged to 4.7 liters and mounted directly to the chassis. With an output of 512.8 HP and 347.2 ft-lb of torque, the car could accelerate from zero to 62.1 mph in just 3.87 seconds and reach a top speed of 201.9 mph.
car3362.hero: This Italian masterpiece, equipped with a naturally-aspirated V-12 and Formula 1 technology, celebrated Ferrari's 50th anniversary.

car3363.desc: This car was a staple of the 1950s race scene. Starting with the base DB3, this car underwent extensive modifications, including a shortened wheelbase, reduced body weight, and refined aerodynamics. Its inline-6 engine, which originally produced 224.9 HP, was later tuned to deliver up to 239.6 HP. It was awarded the Gran Turismo Trophy at Pebble Beach in 2013.
car3363.hero: This historic 1950s race car won the Pebble Beach Gran Turismo Trophy.

car3364.desc: This car was the winner of the GT Award at SEMA 2015. Built by actor Sung Kang, it started with a 1973 Nissan 240Z as its foundation. It was powered by an RB26DETT engine sourced from a GT-R, which was converted to natural aspiration and tuned to produce 216 HP. The car’s aggressive styling was enhanced with wide over-fenders and front and rear spoilers crafted by Rocket Bunny.
car3364.hero: This "poisonous" 240Z, which won the 2015 GT Award, packed a naturally-aspirated RB26 engine.

car3365.desc: Porsche’s first mass-produced sports car made its debut in 1949. From 1955 to 1959, these models were referred to as the 356 A, using an engine derived from the 550 Spyder. The semi-competition 1500 GS GT Carrera, producing 108.5 HP, marked the beginning of the Carrera legacy.
car3365.hero: With the introduction of this model, Porsche became known as a maker of the world's finest sports cars.
car3365.nameLong: Porsche 356 A/1500 GS GT Carrera Speedster '56

car3367.desc: The Toyota Supra made its long-awaited return in 2019, following its discontinuation in 2002. The new model retained an inline-6 engine and rear-wheel-drive layout, embodying the essence of a pure sports car. It featured an ideal 50:50 front-to-rear weight distribution and a low center of gravity, delivering superb balance and driving dynamics. A twin-scroll turbocharger ensured strong, responsive acceleration, while its wide stance and short wheelbase contributed to nimble, agile handling, making it a truly compelling performance machine.
car3367.hero: Toyota's flagship FR sports car returned after a 17-year absence with a completely new look.

car3368.desc: The Tundra was a full-size pickup truck developed by Toyota specifically for the North American market. Introduced in 2015, the TRD Pro variant featured a 5.7-liter V-8 and was specially tuned by Toyota’s motorsports division, TRD. Its suspension was refined with the addition of Fox dampers, while a newly designed hood scoop and BBS wheels enhanced its aggressive appearance.
car3368.hero: Toyota's large pickup was equipped with a unique suspension system to maximize its sporting performance.

car3369.desc: The Radical SR3 SL was a road-legal track machine that closely resembled a scaled-down Le Mans Prototype. Among its powertrain options was a 2.0-liter Ford EcoBoost inline-4 with direct injection and a turbocharger, producing 295.9 HP and paired with a 6-speed sequential paddle-shift transmission. With a curb weight of just 1709 lbs, the SR3 SL delivered remarkable performance, launching from zero to 59.7 mph in just 3.4 seconds and reaching a top speed of 159.7 mph.
car3369.hero: The road-going racer that can handle both pleasure cruises and circuit laps.

car3370.desc: The original Fit Hybrid debuted in 2010, drawing considerable attention as the first hybrid offering in the B-segment. In 2013, the second-generation Fit Hybrid arrived, built upon the third-generation Fit platform. This updated model featured the Sport Hybrid i-DCD system, paired with a 1.5-liter i-VTEC engine to deliver a combined 137.1 HP. In Japan’s JC08 fuel efficiency cycle, it achieved an impressive rating of 85.7 MPG.
car3370.hero: The third-generation hybrid Fit utilized i-DCD to maximize energy efficiency.

car3371.desc: The Japanese Super Formula series transitioned to the Dallara SF19 chassis in 2019. Equipped with a halo system that met F1 safety standards, the SF19 also featured aerodynamic enhancements over its predecessor, the SF14, making overtaking easier and improving race action. Power came from a turbocharged 2.0-liter direct-injection inline-4, with separate versions independently developed by Toyota and Honda. Despite tight regulations, a fierce development battle unfolded between the two manufacturers.
car3371.hero: Both Toyota and Honda provide engines for the Super Formula series. This is the one from Toyota.

car3372.desc: The Japanese Super Formula series transitioned to the Dallara SF19 chassis in 2019. Equipped with a halo system that met F1 safety standards, the SF19 also featured aerodynamic enhancements over its predecessor, the SF14, making overtaking easier and improving race action. Power came from a turbocharged 2.0-liter direct-injection inline-4, with separate versions independently developed by Toyota and Honda. Despite tight regulations, a fierce development battle unfolded between the two manufacturers.
car3372.hero: Both Toyota and Honda provide engines for the Super Formula series. This is the one from Honda.

car3373.desc: The Porsche 962 C was a prototype race car that made its debut in the World Endurance Championship (WEC) in 1985. Over the course of its career, the car delivered Porsche numerous race victories and championship titles. In its debut WEC season, it won seven out of ten races. The following year, in 1986, it claimed four wins from nine rounds in the newly renamed World Sports Prototype Championship (WSPC). At the 1987 WSPC, it secured a win at Le Mans and followed it up with a 2nd-place finish the year after.
car3373.hero: These Group C cars scored numerous endurance racing championships for Porsche.

car3374.desc: The X2019 Competition was developed at the inception of the Gran Turismo Championship, with the goal of creating a race car that was as thrilling to watch as it was to drive. Based on the X2014 Standard, it featured revised design elements, including new front wheel styling, a reworked rear body structure, and reshaped rear wheel covers. Also, the powertrain was updated from a turbocharged 2.0-liter engine to a naturally-aspirated 3.0-liter unit, and the throttle system was replaced with a more conventional mechanical setup.
car3374.hero: This is an evolution of the X2014 created for the FIA Gran Turismo Championships.
car3374.nameLong: Gran Turismo Red Bull X2019 Competition

car3375.desc: Launched in 1949, the 356 A was a refined successor to Porsche’s first production model, the 356. Two variants were offered, both using a detuned version of the 550 Spyder’s engine. The 1500 GS Carrera road-going version produced 98.6 HP, while the semi-competition 1500 GS GT delivered 108.5 HP. This model also introduced the "Carrera" name—now synonymous with Porsche performance.
car3375.hero: A semi-race equipped model of the 356A, one of the cars that contributed to the Porsche mystique.

car3376.desc: The Jaguar D-Type was a racing sports car introduced in 1954 as the successor to the C-Type, with just 64 units produced in total. It's built on a tubular frame with monocoque construction. Its sleek bodywork, penned by Malcolm Sayer, was instantly recognizable by the aerodynamic fin positioned behind the driver’s seat. It made its debut at the 1954 24 Hours of Le Mans and went on to dominate the event, securing victory three years in a row through 1957.
car3376.hero: With three consecutive victories at Le Mans, this racing Jaguar featured a large fin that helped lateral stability at high speed.

car3377.desc: The Dodge Super Bee was introduced in 1968 as a performance-focused yet affordable muscle car. It offered a range of powerful engine options, with the 7.0-liter V-8 producing 425 HP at the top of the lineup. True to its purpose, the car came with minimal comfort features. A facelifted version appeared in 1970, followed by the second-generation model in 1971, which was based on the Charger.
car3377.hero: A Coronet, equipped with a 7.0-liter V8 Hemi, this was one of the standout cars in the muscle-car era.

car3383.desc: The Mazda Demio underwent a full model change in 2014, entering its fourth generation with a bold new direction. Adopting Mazda’s KODO design philosophy, it showcased styling sharp enough to rival its European counterparts. One of its standout features was the newly developed turbocharged 1.5-liter diesel engine, the SKYACTIV-D 1.5. Praised for its excellent fuel efficiency, the diesel variant quickly gained popularity, accounting for more than 60 percent of total orders.
car3383.hero: This compact diesel model from Mazda offered more luxury than you would expect from a car in its class.

car3384.desc: Introduced in 1990, the GTO marked Mitsubishi’s return to the true sports car segment after many years. Its bold, wide-bodied styling was clearly aimed at the American market. The car packed a suite of advanced technologies for its time, including all-wheel control, 4-wheel steering, electronically controlled suspension, and active aerodynamic elements. Under the hood was a 3.0-liter V-6 engine, offered in both naturally-aspirated and twin-turbocharged forms. It was sold overseas as the 3000GT, where it gained popularity for its bold styling and aggressive performance.
car3384.hero: This pure-bred sports car by Mitsubishi featured advanced AWD technology.

car3385.desc: Introduced in 1975, the 911 Turbo was the first production Porsche to wear the now-iconic "Turbo" badge. True to its name, the car’s 3.0L air-cooled flat-6 engine was equipped with a KKK turbocharger, producing 256.4 HP. This setup enabled the car to cruise at speeds of up to 155.3 mph—a remarkable feat for its era. Beginning in 1977, the engine’s displacement was increased to 3.3 liters and paired with an air-to-air intercooler, which further boosted performance.
car3385.hero: This top-of-the-line version of the vaunted 911 possessed a more muscular look and a turbocharged engine.

car3387.desc: The sixth-generation Chevrolet Camaro made its debut in 2015. At the top of the lineup stood the ZL1, powered by the same supercharged 5.7-liter LT4 V-8 engine found in the Corvette Z06. It delivered an impressive 649.9 HP and 649.5 ft-lb of torque. In 2018, a version equipped with the 1LE performance package—which included upgrades to the suspension and drivetrain—recorded a Nürburgring lap time of 7:16.04, outperforming a number of supercars.
car3387.hero: This version of the sixth-generation Camaro lived up to the hype, thanks in part to its 649.9 HP LT1 engine.

car3388.desc: Mercedes-AMG created this touring car in its early years. The 300 SEL 6.3 was already quick, but AMG bored the engine out to 6.8 liters and re-tuned it, raising output from 246.5 HP to 422.1 HP. At the 1971 24 Hours of Spa, it took 1st in class and 2nd overall—an early showcase of AMG’s racing pedigree.
car3388.hero: This legendary race car put AMG on the map after its class victory at the 1971 24 Hours of Spa.

car3389.desc: The third-generation M3 was introduced with the E46 3 Series. Its 3.2-liter S54 Inline-6 delivered more than 98.6 HP per liter, peaking at 338.3 HP at 7900 rpm. In 2003, the high-performance CSL variant was launched. It featured a carbon-fiber roof to reduce weight and a retuned engine pushing output to 355 HP. This model went on to achieve significant success in touring car racing and various other motorsport events.
car3389.hero: Featuring BMW's high-revving engine technology, this sports car represented the epitome of the E46 3 Series.

car3390.desc: The Taycan marked Porsche’s first fully electric sports sedan. Equipped with electric motors on the front and rear axles, its advanced all-wheel-drive system was paired with a 2-speed transmission, delivering blistering acceleration and top-end performance. The overboost-equipped Turbo S variant produced 560 kW (750.5 HP). Notably, the Taycan was the first mass-produced vehicle to feature an 800V electrical system, enhancing both powertrain efficiency and reducing charging times.
car3390.hero: With a total system voltage of 800V, this fully electric sedan boasts both comfort and remarkable performance.

car3391.desc: The original GT350R was developed for race competition in 1965, based on the original Mustang. The 2016 Shelby GT350R was similarly based on the seventh generation Mustang, with the engine tuned to 525.6 HP. The chassis components supporting the engine performance were also upgraded, resulting in a car that was fit to go to the circuit straight from the factory.
car3391.hero: This high-performance model of the seventh-generation Mustang takes its name from a legend.

car3392.desc: Lamborghini’s flagship models had long featured V-12 engines, but their most extreme variants carried the Superveloce (SV) badge. Translated as "super fast" in Italian, the designation traced its origins back to the legendary Miura. The Aventador SV variant was introduced in 2015, delivering 49.3 HP more than the base model for a total output of 739.6 HP.
car3392.hero: The top-of-the-line version of the Aventador wore the revered SV badge.

car3393.desc: The Porsche Carrera GT was a mid-engine super sports car produced from 2003 to 2006, with a total of 1,270 units built. Its chassis centered on a lightweight yet rigid carbon-fiber monocoque, complemented by carbon fiber subframes supporting the engine and rear suspension. Power came from a naturally-aspirated 5.7-liter V-10, derived from a race engine, producing 603.5 HP. This was paired with a 6-speed manual gearbox.
car3393.hero: Only 1270 examples of this mid-engine supercar were produced from 2003 to 2006.

car3394.desc: The Aston Martin DBR9 GT1 was developed by Aston Martin Racing in 2005 for competition in the GT1 category, based on the road-going DB9. Its body was significantly lightened using carbon-fiber construction, and it was powered by a 5.9-liter V-12 engine paired with a 6-speed sequential transmission. The DBR9 made an immediate impact, winning its debut race at the 12 Hours of Sebring. It went on to secure GT1 class victories at the 24 Hours of Le Mans in both 2007 and 2008.
car3394.hero: This GT1 race car based on the Aston Martin DB9, commemorated the marque's return to international motorsports.

car3395.desc: This car was produced by Caterham in 1996, more than two decades after the company inherited production rights to the Seven from Lotus in 1973. As the Superlight name implied, weight was trimmed throughout the car, making it between 77 lbs and 110 lbs lighter than the standard Seven, depending on trim. The later models from 2008 and after, were powered by a 2.0-liter Ford engine producing 262.3 HP, giving it 0-to-62.1 mph acceleration of 2.88 seconds and performance that could rival supercars.
car3395.hero: The ultimate version of the extremely lightweight Caterham.

car3396.desc: This Vision Gran Turismo was created by Jaguar Advanced Design. A fully electric model, it carries forward the legacy of Jaguar’s legendary race cars like the C-type, D-type, and E-type, not only in elegance, but also in engineering, with a low center of mass and near-perfect weight distribution. Inside the cockpit, all essential driving information has been seamlessly projected ahead of the driver, delivering a thrilling racing experience through advanced digital integration.
car3396.hero: This fully electric sports car combines Jaguar's rich racing tradition with the latest in EV technology.

car3397.desc: To compete in the newly established FIA GT Championship in 1997, Mercedes-Benz and AMG developed the CLK-GTR in just 128 days. Equipped with a V-12 engine, the car proved immediately successful, securing both the team and driver championships in its debut season. The following year, Mercedes introduced the CLK-LM as an evolution model. It made its debut at the 24 Hours of Le Mans, going on to dominate the FIA GT Championship, winning all 10 rounds and clinching the season title.
car3397.hero: Making the switch from a heavy V12 engine to a lighter V8 helped this Mercedes-Benz dominate the FIA GT championship.

car3398.desc: Released in 2007, the RUF CTR3 served as the successor to the iconic CTR and CTR2. Unlike its predecessors, which were based on the Porsche 930 and 993 Turbo, the CTR3 was designed entirely from the ground up by RUF. It adopted a mid-engine layout and was powered by a twin-turbocharged 3.8-liter flat-6 with intercooling. Performance was staggering, with a top speed of 236.1 mph and zero-62.1 mph acceleration in just 3.2 seconds.
car3398.hero: The third-generation CTR was thoroughly re-engineered by Ruf, including being converted to a mid-engine layout.

car3399.desc: The GR Supra marked the return of Toyota’s flagship sports car, 17 years after production ended. It retained a rear-wheel-drive layout and inline-6, but came wrapped in a modern two-seat body with advanced construction and a twin-scroll turbocharger. It made its Nürburgring 24 Hours debut in 2018 and, in 2019, finished 3rd in the SP8T class and 41st overall. This cementing its image as a true performance contender.
car3399.hero: The Supra returned after a 17-year hiatus, with this racing version competing at the Nürburgring in 2019.

car3400.desc: Porsche also developed the 911 GT1 Strassenversion—a road-legal counterpart to the 911 GT1 race car built for GT competition between 1996 and 1998. While the headlights were updated to match those of the Type 996, the core construction of the car remained nearly identical to its racing sibling. To comply with emissions regulations, the engine was detuned to 536.5 HP, yet the car still managed a 0–62.1 mph sprint in just 3.7 seconds and reached a top speed of 191.4 mph.
car3400.hero: A road-going version of the 911 GT1 was developed by Porsche to compete in GT racing.

car3401.desc: In 2012, the Toyota Crown underwent a full model change, entering its 14th generation with a bold new front-end design. The lineup was split into two distinct versions: the more conservative "Royal" and the sportier "Athlete." The Royal featured design elements inspired by a crown, while the Athlete adopted a more aggressive look with lightning bolt motifs. Together, they introduced a fresh visual identity while preserving the core values that had defined the Crown nameplate for generations.
car3401.hero: The 14th-generation Crown sported a bold front-end design, giving the sport sedan an extra dose of flair.

car3402.desc: Between 2005 and 2006, Ford produced the GT, a modern homage to the legendary GT40. A decade later, in 2015, a second-generation model was unveiled. While retaining the unmistakable lineage of the GT40, it introduced an aggressively aerodynamic form and cutting-edge engineering. Built around a carbon-fiber monocoque with aluminum subframes, it was significantly lighter and delivered a top speed of 216.2 mph.
car3402.hero: The second-generation Ford GT came complete with reengineered aerodynamics.

car3403.desc: Released in 1974, the Volkswagen Golf quickly rose to popularity as a pioneer of the compact car segment. The sporty GTI variant featured a 1.6-liter inline-4 SOHC engine with Bosch fuel injection, producing 108.5 HP. Blending performance with everyday practicality, the GTI redefined the concept of sporty driving.
car3403.hero: This grandfather of hot hatches balanced everyday usability with a fun-to-drive nature.

car3404.desc: The fourth-generation Type 993 Porsche 911 was introduced as an all-new model in 1993. In 1995, the Carrera RS followed, featuring a lighter yet more rigid body and a 295.9 HP 3.8-liter flat-6 engine. The lineup also included the track-focused Carrera RS Clubsport. Specifically designed for circuit use, it came equipped with a large front spoiler, a prominent rear wing, and a welded roll cage.
car3404.hero: This version of the Type 993, the final air-cooled Porsche 911, was designed specifically for the race track.

car3405.desc: This was the evolution model of the R8 LMS. Cooling efficiency and aerodynamic performance saw notable improvements over its predecessor, while the entire drivetrain was upgraded to boost reliability under the demands of endurance racing. Although engine output remained unchanged, a 55 lbs reduction in body weight allowed greater flexibility in weight distribution through ballast adjustment. Making its debut in the autumn of 2018, the car demonstrated its potential with a victory at the Gulf 12 Hours later that year.
car3405.hero: This evolved version of Audi's R8 LMS competed in various GT3 events across the globe.

car3406.desc: Introduced in 2014, the Charger SRT Hellcat stands as one of the most powerful and extreme models in the Charger’s long-running legacy, which dates back to 1966. Developed by SRT, Chrysler’s high-performance division, the car produces 707.1 HP and reaches a top speed of 204 mph. This safety car version is a Gran Turismo Original model.
car3406.hero: This ultra high performance Charger set a world speed record, going 222 mph on the Bonneville Salt Flats.
car3406.nameLong: Dodge Charger SRT Hellcat Safety Car

car3407.desc: This fictional safety car is based on that very Mégane R.S. Trophy. Developed by Renault Sport, the "R.S." was the high-performance version of the Mégane, but the Trophy edition pushed even further with increased engine output and finely tuned suspension, all in pursuit of becoming the fastest front-wheel-drive production car in the world.
car3407.hero: This safety car version of the Mégane RS Trophy was created to patrol the race track.
car3407.nameLong: Renault Sport Mégane R.S. Trophy Safety Car

car3408.desc: In 2012, the Toyota Crown underwent a full model change, entering its 14th generation with a bold new front-end design. The lineup was split into two distinct versions: the more conservative "Royal" and the sportier "Athlete." Four different powertrains were offered across the series: a 3.5-liter V-6, a 2.5-liter V-6, a 2.5-liter inline-4 hybrid, and a 2.0-liter inline-4 turbo. This safety car version was a Gran Turismo Original design.
car3408.hero: This Crown Athlete, converted into a safety car, was designed to patrol the race track.
car3408.nameLong: Toyota Crown Athlete G Safety Car

car3409.desc: Built by Britain’s Briggs Automotive Company, this car was designed to deliver “the most authentic and pure driving experience” on the road. Its single-seat layout is built around a tubular chassis wrapped in a carbon-fiber shell, and it’s powered by a Cosworth-tuned 2.5-liter Ford Duratec engine. Weighing just 1279 lbs, the car rockets from 0-60 mph in a blistering 2.8 seconds, and reaches a top speed of 170.3 mph—performance figures on par with a Formula 3 car.
car3409.hero: Simple yet effective, this single-seat sports car is reminiscent of formula cars from a bygone era.

car3410.desc: The 917K was a prototype race car developed by Porsche specifically for sports car competition. Despite weighing under 1764 lbs, the 1970 version was capable of producing up to 591.7 HP in its most powerful configuration. In its second year of competition, 1970, the 917K proved nearly unbeatable, winning seven out of ten rounds in the International Championship for Makes. It also delivered Porsche its long-awaited first overall victory at the 24 Hours of Le Mans.
car3410.hero: This prototype race car that gave Porsche its first victory at the 24 Hours of Le Mans.

car3411.desc: In 2020, Alfa Romeo marked their 110th anniversary with the release of the special Giulia GTA and GTAm models. The twin-turbo 2.9-liter V-6 saw its output raised to 532.5 HP, accompanied by weight reduction and a wider track for enhanced performance. The GTAm, built with circuit driving in mind, featured a large front splitter, carbon fiber rear wing, and integrated roll bars—delivering a truly hardcore setup.
car3411.hero: The top-of-the-line model in the Giulia lineup celebrated 110 years of Alfa Romeo.

car3412.desc: The second-generation model of Audi’s road car, bearing the name of its renowned Le Mans prototype, continued the legacy of performance and innovation. While preserving the silhouette of its predecessor, the new model introduced a revised Audi Space Frame for improved rigidity and reduced weight, alongside an updated quattro all-wheel-drive system. The V10 Plus represented the high-performance model, with its 5.2-liter V-10 engine further refined to deliver an impressive 601.6 HP. It came equipped with a fixed rear wing and a mechanical LSD as standard.
car3412.hero: Audi's second-generation sports car based on the Le Mans-conquering R8.

car3413.desc: In 2017, Subaru introduced the BRZ STI Sport as the flagship of the BRZ lineup. It was co-developed with Subaru’s motorsports division, STI (Subaru Tecnica International). The most notable upgrade was the revised chassis setup. Handling and stability were enhanced through STI’s proprietary Flexible V-Bar and Flexible Draw Stiffener components, while custom-developed suspension parts boosted overall agility.
car3413.hero: Numerous chassis performance and visual enhancements by STI gave the BRZ sports car unprecedented flair.

car3414.desc: This Vision Gran Turismo concept was born from the passion and technical expertise of the team at Centro Stile Lamborghini. Built around Lamborghini’s signature design language, highlighted by bold "Y" elements and hexagonal forms, it also pays tribute to the iconic Stratos Zero with a side profile that echoed its striking silhouette. Power comes from a V-12 engine paired with a supercapacitor-based hybrid system, derived from the Sián FKP 37. In a refined detail, part of this advanced system is visible from the outside, blending high-performance engineering with unmistakable style.
car3414.hero: This futuristic single-seat sports concept possesses the core concepts of Lamborghini's design DNA.

car3415.desc: As its name suggested, the Alfa Romeo 8C 2900B Touring Berlinetta was a stunning coupe, its body hand-shaped by Carrozzeria Touring using the lightweight superleggera method. The "8C" badge referred to the car’s 8-cylinder engine. Designed by the legendary Vittorio Jano, the water-cooled inline-8 delivered performance that placed the machine firmly in race-car territory. It's believed that only five examples were ever produced.
car3415.hero: Equipped with DOHC V-8, this exquisite coupe was produced by Alfa Romeo in the pre-war period.

car3416.desc: This was a true “road-going race car” derived from the AMG GT. Its aggressive wide-body design included flared fenders and an active aerodynamic system, while the front grille featured bold vertical slats that echoed AMG’s motorsport DNA. Under the hood, the twin-turbo 4.0-liter V-8 had been tuned to deliver an impressive 576.9 HP and 515.7 ft-lb of torque. It also marked a technical milestone, becoming the first Mercedes-AMG model to feature 4-wheel steering.
car3416.hero: This 'road-legal race car' evokes the image of the much-celebrated 300SL sports car.

car3417.desc: Jaguar’s second Vision Gran Turismo was developed with engineering input from Jaguar Special Vehicles (SV). While retaining its elegant silhouette, the car received a complete aerodynamic overhaul to maximize downforce. The powertrain features four electric motors, drawing from Jaguar’s Formula E expertise. The battery system utilizes state-of-the-art liquid nitrogen cooling.
car3417.hero: This virtual electric race car provides a glimpse into the future of Jaguar.

car3418.desc: The Toyota Supra made its long-awaited return in 2019, following its discontinuation in 2002. The new model retained an inline-6 engine and rear-wheel-drive layout, embodying the essence of a pure sports car. It featured an ideal 50:50 front-to-rear weight distribution and a low center of gravity, delivering superb balance and driving dynamics. A twin-scroll turbocharger ensured strong, responsive acceleration, while its wide stance and short wheelbase contributed to nimble, agile handling, making it a truly compelling performance machine.
car3418.hero: The 2020 Supra possessed a significant power boost compared to the past model.

car3419.desc: The RX-VISION concept was introduced at the 2015 Tokyo Motor Show. The base car’s elegant proportions have been reimagined with a more aggressive, motorsport-focused edge. To meet the performance demands of the Gr.3 class, the lightweight body houses a 4-rotor engine, drawing inspiration from the legendary 787B powerplant, revived through cutting-edge SKYACTIV technology to deliver unprecedented levels of power and responsiveness.

car3420.desc: Introduced in 2018, the fourth-generation Ford Focus included a high-performance RS variant in its lineup. This iteration marked the first time the RS featured 4-wheel drive, complete with adjustable torque distribution for enhanced handling. New selectable drive modes, such as "Track" and "Drift," were introduced, complementing an improved chassis and damping system. At its core was a 2.3-liter inline-4 EcoBoost engine producing 345.2 HP. With a zero–62.1 mph time of 4.7 seconds and a top speed of 165.3 mph, the car delivered remarkable performance in a compact package.
car3420.hero: The RS model of the third-generation Ford Focus was the first to get 4-wheel drive.

car3421.desc: This mid-engine sports car made its debut in 1972 as the sister to the Bora. While the Bora was equipped with a V-8, the Merak utilized a smaller 3.0-liter V-6 sourced from the Citroën SM, allowing a 2+2 seating layout by making use of the extra space freed up in the rear. The SS was a high-performance variant introduced in 1975. By increasing the engine’s compression ratio, output was boosted, raising the top speed from 139.8 mph to 155.3 mph.
car3421.hero: This high-output model of the Merak has been tuned for even sharper performance.

car3422.desc: Unveiled in 1971, the 3.0 CSL served as the homologation version of the BMW 3.0 CS, featuring a powerful 3.0-liter inline-6 engine. Engine displacement grew from 2985 cc to 3003 cc in 1972, and to 3155 cc in 1973 for the evolution models, which achieved remarkable success on the European touring car stage.
car3422.hero: This lightweight model of the BMW 3.0 CS was developed to compete in touring car racing.

car3423.desc: The Gran Turismo Award was presented to standout custom cars showcased at SEMA. In 2016, the 14th award went to the Wicked Fabrications GT 51—a 1951 Ford Custom Club Coupe crafted by a team of specialists for former racing driver Bruce Leven. The project required an estimated 10,000 hours to complete.
car3423.hero: More than 10,000 labor hours went into this 2016 Gran Turismo Award winner.

car3424.desc: The Lancer Evolution IX GSR bears the MR initials for Mitsubishi Racing. Performance was enhanced in every area. The MIVEC system was tuned to sharpen turbo response, while the suspension benefited from Eibach springs and an updated AYC calibration for improved cornering stability. Marking the final appearance of the legendary 4G63 engine, this model stood as the pinnacle of the third wave of Lancer Evolution cars.
car3424.nameLong: Mitsubishi Lancer Evolution IX MR GSR '06

car3426.desc: This machine was the winner of the 2014 Gran Turismo Award. A heavily customized 1970 Chevrolet Camaro SS, it was reimagined by Roadster Shop in Illinois, USA. The car’s structure was rebuilt from the ground up using lightweight carbon fiber and aluminum components, while under the hood sat a rear-offset 7.0-liter LS7 engine tuned to produce 739.6 HP. Its aggressive aesthetic was matched by performance, with wide overfenders, a bold front spoiler, and a prominent rear wing.
car3426.hero: This 2014 GT Awards winner was a high-speed monster wearing the skin of a Camaro SS.

car3427.desc: Introduced in 2011, this marked the final special edition of the Mazda RX-8. Built on the 6-speed manual Type RS—equipped with Bilstein dampers—and the 6-speed automatic Type E—offering upscale touches like leather seating—both variants received exclusive interior and exterior enhancements. Initially planned as a 1,000-unit production, strong demand following the announcement of the RX-8’s discontinuation in 2012 prompted Mazda to double the run with an additional 1,000 units.
car3427.hero: The final version of the RX-8, Mazda's rotary engine sports car with a unique 4-door layout.

car3428.desc: This car earned double honors at the 2017 Pebble Beach Concours d’Elegance, capturing both Best of Show and the Gran Turismo Trophy. Produced between 1926 and 1933, what many regard as Mercedes-Benz’s first true sports car was the vision of Ferdinand Porsche. Powered by a supercharged 7.0-liter inline-6, it was wrapped in elegant "boat tail" coachwork crafted by Barker.
car3428.hero: This very unqiue sports car was the first from Mercedes-Benz and is known for its characteristic boat tail styling.

car3429.desc: Introduced in 1969 as the top-grade variant of the Fairlady Z, the Z 432 was powered by the S20 inline-6 DOHC engine, producing 157.8 HP. Based on the powerplant of Nissan’s R380 race car, the engine gave the car a zero-to-1312.3 ft time of 15.8 seconds and registered a top speed of 130.5 mph. The Z 432 also proved itself in competitive racing. A lightweight version—the Z 432 R—was produced in limited numbers, featuring fiberglass panels and acrylic components to shed weight.
car3429.hero: This special Datsun Z was equipped with the same engine as the Skyline GT-R.

car3430.desc: The roots of the SUV category could be traced back to this compact 4-wheel-drive vehicle, developed at the request of the U.S. military in 1940. Among the prototypes submitted by Bantam, Ford, and Willys, it was the Willys MB—an improved version of the MA—that proved to be the winner, ultimately leading to the production of over 360,000 units. Its straightforward yet durable construction, featuring a ladder frame, rigid axles, and 4-wheel drive, resulted in a truly historic vehicle whose legacy has endured for generations.
car3430.hero: The U.S. Army-commissioned vehicle that became the forefather of the modern SUV.

car3431.desc: In 1989, Porsche introduced the third-generation 911, known internally as the Type 964. Although it retained the familiar shape of its predecessor, it was a major leap forward, with about 80 percent of its components being newly developed. The Carrera 4, featuring 4-wheel drive, debuted first, followed by the rear-wheel-drive Carrera 2 in 1990. The Carrera RS of this generation was a performance-tuned variant based on the Carrera 2.
car3431.hero: This Porsche was a lighter version of the third-generation 911 Carrera 2 and came with a 3.6-liter flat-6.

car3432.desc: The first facelift of the GD-generation Impreza was marked by its distinctive teardrop-shaped “blob eye” headlights. Engine efficiency was improved with the adoption of equal-length, matched exhaust headers. Also, some manual variants featured a Driver's Control Center Differential with an automatic mode. A minor update in 2004 brought larger tires and boosted torque output to 303.8 ft-lb.
car3432.hero: The second-generation Impreza was developed alongside the rally spec model.

car3433.desc: The FXX K, a track-only evolution of the LaFerrari, was produced in a limited run of just 32 units in 2014. It pairs the LaFerrari’s 6.3-liter V12 with a 187.4 HP electric motor, delivering a combined output of 1035.5 HP. With enhanced aerodynamics—further amplified by the optional EVO kit, which adds 75 percent more downforce. Free from the constraints of racing regulations, this car delivers pure, uncompromised driving performance at its highest level.
car3433.hero: The production run of this Ferrari was limited to only 32 units.

car3434.desc: Unveiled in 1984, the Testarossa stood as Ferrari’s flagship mid-engine masterpiece. Its heart was a 5.0-liter 180-degree V-12, delivering a maximum output of 384.6 HP and torque of 361.6 ft-lb. Acceleration from zero to 62.1 mph took just 5.8 seconds, with the car ultimately achieving a top speed of 180.2 mph. With its sculpted form—defined by signature 5-fin strakes and rear fenders that flared boldly from the tight cockpit—the Testarossa captivated a new generation of enthusiasts.
car3434.hero: This historic Ferrari flagship impressed all with its vivid design.

car3436.desc: Unveiled in 2015, the second-generation Ford GT focused on aerodynamics and speed, with a compact twin-turbo V-6 engine delivering zero–to -62.1 mph in 3.0 seconds and a top speed of 216.2 mph. In racing, Chip Ganassi Racing represented the United States in both the FIA World Endurance Championship and IMSA starting in 2016.
car3436.hero: This race car claimed numerous World Endurance Championship titles.

car3437.desc: This was De Tomaso’s second production mid-engine sports car. To address the lack of power in the earlier Vallelunga, it was fitted with a Ford V-8 engine. Weighing approximately 1.3 tons, the car could reach a top speed of 155.3 mph, thanks to its lightweight construction. The exterior, notable for its gullwing-opening rear section, was designed by Giorgetto Giugiaro during his time at Carrozzeria Ghia. Production was limited to just 401 units.
car3437.hero: This mid-engine sports car set the stage for the famous Pantera.

car3438.desc: The FIAT Abarth 595 made its debut in 1963. It was derived from the second-generation FIAT 500 tuned by Abarth. An even more potent variant of the 595 later emerged as the 595 Esseesse. While it retained the same engine displacement, engineers raised compression to boost output to 31.6 HP. Thanks to this added performance, the 595 lineup made its mark in European racing, dominating the under 600 cc category.
car3438.hero: A hardcore sports version of the FIAT 500.

car3439.desc: Porsche introduced the fourth-generation 911 in 1993 with the launch of the Type 993. Alongside revised styling, the model featured significant suspension improvements that enhanced handling. The most powerful variant of the series was the Carrera RS, released in 1995, which featured a more rigid yet lighter body. Powering the car was the final air-cooled engine used in the 911—a 3.8-liter flat-6 producing 295.9 HP. The track-focused Carrera RS Clubsport was also made available.
car3439.hero: The most powerful version of the 993, the last air-cooled Porsche, came with a 3.8-liter flat-6 producing 295.9 HP.

car3440.desc: The 964 represented the third generation of the 911 series, following the Type 901 and 930. The lineup included a “Turbo” model for those seeking greater performance, as well as the 911 Turbo S Leichtbau, a special variant created to commemorate Porsche’s success in the 1993 IMSA series. True to its “Leichtbau” (lightweight) name, the Turbo S featured high-lift camshafts and a revised turbocharger with increased boost, producing 375.7 HP/361.6 ft-lb. Weight was also significantly reduced compared with the standard Turbo model.
car3440.hero: The third-generation 911 Turbo was virtually all new with 80 percent new parts.

car3441.desc: The 300 SL race car, known inhouse as W194, used a tubular frame with aluminum body panels, paired with modified mechanicals from the W186 300. The car’s debut at the 1952 24 Hours of Le Mans resulted in a landmark win for Mercedes-Benz. That success sparked public demand, ultimately leading to the production of the 300 SL road car.
car3441.hero: The car that brought Mercedes-Benz its first victory at the 24 Hours of Le Mans.

car3442.desc: The A112 Abarth, introduced in 1971, was widely regarded as one of the original hot hatches. Based on the Autobianchi A112, the car was tuned by Abarth. Continuously refined throughout its production run, the car's engine displacement was increased in 1975, raising output to 70 HP, and in 1979, a 5-speed transmission was added. Although production ended in 1985, the A112 Abarth maintained a loyal following among enthusiasts drawn to its lively character.
car3442.hero: The original hot hatch, with excellent power and agile handling, paved the way for a new genre.

car3443.desc: Introduced in 1975, the 308 GTB replaced the Dino 246 GT and launched Ferrari’s long-running series of V-8-powered two-seaters. Its elegant body, laid over a steel-tube frame, was designed by Leonardo Fioravanti of Pininfarina, the mind behind many of Ferrari’s most celebrated shapes from the 1960s through the early 1990s.
car3443.hero: This successor to the Ferrari Dino 246 GT features a V-8 mounted amidships.

car3444.desc: The car’s spirit is deeply rooted in American custom car and hot rod culture, a tradition that traces back to the 1930s. Model T and Model B Fords were often boldly modified, with exterior customizations and engine swaps for more powerful units. The V-3883, displayed in the Henry Ford Museum, features a Chrysler 331 Hemi engine producing 177.5 HP. A relatively simple yet striking example, its exposed engine cover serves as a key visual accent, capturing the essence of early American hot rod craftsmanship.
car3444.hero: This "High Boy"-style hot rod was displayed at the Henry Ford Museum.

car3445.desc: The DB5 was a sports car introduced by Aston Martin in 1963. Designed by Italy’s Carrozzeria Touring, it featured superleggera construction that helped reduce overall weight. The standard model’s engine produced 282 horsepower (281.1 HP), while the Vantage variant delivered 314 horsepower (313.6 HP). It was praised as one of the standout sports cars of the early 1960s. It also gained iconic status as one of the original “Bond cars,” famously appearing in the James Bond 007 film series.
car3445.hero: This classic sports car from the 1960s, as well as its most famous driver, James Bond, put Aston Martin on the international sports-car map.

car3446.desc: First sold in 1954, the 550/1500RS was a racing sports car featuring a lightweight aluminum body over a steel tube frame, powered by a 4-cam flat-4 engine producing 133.1 HP. It delivered impressive results on the track, securing class victories at the 24 Hours of Le Mans in both 1954 and 1955. This particular 1500RS is especially prized, still wearing the original paint it sported during the 1956 running of Le Mans.
car3446.hero: This French blue Porsche wears the original livery from the 1956 24 Hours of Le Mans race.

car3447.desc: The Vantage proved to be a success as a performance-focused, rear-wheel-drive sports car. The model introduced in 2017 shared much of its construction with the DB11 V8, but featured a shorter wheelbase and was approximately 265 lbs lighter. These changes earned it widespread acclaim, with many praising it as the best-handling Aston Martin to date. The engine was a Mercedes-AMG–derived twin-turbocharged 4.0-liter V-8, capable of reaching a top speed of 195.1 mph (195 mph).
car3447.hero: This lightweight cornering machine has been hailed as the finest Aston Martin ever.

car3449.desc: The ZR1 was introduced near the end of the C7 Corvette’s production run, becoming the most powerful version of the generation. Under the hood, the supercharged 6.2-liter LT5 V-8 delivered 754.4 HP and 969 Nm (714.6 ft-lb) of torque. Its aerodynamic components were developed in collaboration with Pratt & Miller Engineering, which campaigned the C7 in GT racing. Buyers could choose between a model focused on lap times, or one maximizing top speed. A ZR1 equipped with the high-speed package was capable of reaching an impressive 214.9 mph.
car3449.hero: One of the last of the C7 Corvettes and also the most powerful.

car345.desc: This car was the Trueno owned by Shuichi Shigeno, the creator of the acclaimed manga "Initial D," which prominently featured the "Hachi-Roku" AE86 Levin and Trueno models. Fitted with an HKS exhaust manifold and a Trust silencer, its engine was tuned to produce 207.1 HP. A TRD suspension kit was also installed, enabling agile handling and high cornering speeds.
car345.hero: This modified 86 was built to order for the author of the "Initial D" comic books.
car345.nameLong: Toyota Trueno 3door 1600GT APEX (AE86 Shuichi Shigeno Version)

car3450.desc: The Nissan GT-R NISMO GT3 was a production-based race machine built to FIA GT3 regulations, derived from the R35 GT-R. Later iterations were based on the GT-R NISMO, incorporating a dry sump system to lower the center of gravity and optimize weight distribution. Enhanced front-end rigidity and a newly designed suspension setup improved handling response. A revised engine bay layout boosted cooling efficiency, contributing to greater stability at high speeds.
car3450.hero: This racing spec version of the GT-R was created for GT3 category competition.

car3451.desc: Developed by Toyota for the WRC, the GR Yaris may have appeared as a simple compact car, but underneath was a serious competition machine. With increased rigidity, reduced weight, and a dramatically lowered center of gravity, it was engineered for peak performance. The 4-wheel-drive RZ model featured a 1.6-liter 3-cylinder turbo engine paired with a 6-speed manual transmission. The RZ High Performance variant added a limited-slip differential, delivering rock-solid traction. In January 2020, the "1st Edition" was introduced as a special edition model, marking the launch with exclusive features.
car3451.hero: This new WRC race car was created to carry the torch for Toyota's strong rallying tradition.
car3451.nameLong: Toyota GR Yaris 1st Edition RZ "High performance" '20

car3452.desc: The Porsche 917 earned a celebrated place in motorsport history by securing seven victories out of ten races during the 1970 World Sportscar Championship season. The Porsche 917 LIVING LEGEND was a hypercar concept inspired by the 917. Its classic exterior design masked cutting-edge technology beneath the surface. Its blend of top speed and aerodynamic downforce resulted in remarkable stability, even at speeds exceeding 186.4 mph.
car3452.hero: This extreme hyper car is an updated version of the legendary 917, one of the most celebrated race cars in Porsche history.

car3453.desc: This homologation model was developed from the 3 Series platform of its time, specifically to compete in touring car racing. Built on the 2-door sedan, it featured a widened track and aerodynamic enhancements, including an adjustable rear wing to improve performance. It initially came with a 2.3-liter DOHC inline-4 engine, with continuous yearly refinements leading to the 2.5-liter Sport Evolution model.
car3453.hero: A virtual race car for the street, this homologation model once claimed victory in the DTM.

car3454.desc: In 1968, BMW introduced the 2800 CS sports coupe, powered by a robust 2.8-liter inline-6 engine. By 1971, the 3.0 CS arrived, an updated version with a larger engine. To compete in motorsport, BMW created a lightweight homologation model based on the 3.0 CS, naming it the 3.0 CSL. The "L" in CSL stood for “light,” reflecting the car’s reduced weight for racing.
car3454.hero: This lightweight model of the 3.0 CS was stripped of all creature comforts to maximize performance.

car3456.desc: The Swift Sport was the high-performance variant of the fourth-generation Suzuki Swift, launched in 2016. Its aerodynamic body concealed a downsized turbocharged 1.4-liter engine, specially tuned to run on high-octane fuel. The suspension received dedicated tuning to sharpen handling. Notably, this iteration was 154 lbs lighter than its predecessor, contributing to its agility and dynamic driving feel.
car3456.hero: Superb handling was just one of the fortes of this high-performance Japanese hatchback.

car3457.desc: While Alpine earned fame through rallying success with the A110, the 1960s also saw the marque build competitive prototype racers that achieved results on the track. Among them, the A220 stood as Alpine’s strongest contender for overall victory at the 24 Hours of Le Mans, making its debut in 1968. Although the car was beset by mechanical issues and failed to deliver the expected result, it remained a fan favorite and a cherished part of Alpine’s legacy.
car3457.hero: Not only a maker of dominant rally cars, the noted French car company also forayed into road machines.

car3458.desc: This was the high-performance variant of the fourth-generation C-Class. While it carried the familiar C63 name, it introduced significant changes, most notably replacing the naturally-aspirated 6.2-liter V-8 with a more compact and efficient twin-turbocharged 4.0-liter V-8. Shared with the AMG GT, the engine was specially tuned, featuring increased maximum torque and a broader low-end range to better suit the C63’s weight and everyday performance needs. The C63 S Coupé is a circuit-focused performance model.
car3458.hero: The most powerful model of the fourth-generation C-Class boasts a twin-turbocharged 4.0-liter V-8.

car3459.desc: The Porsche 918 Spyder was a high-performance sports car introduced in 2011. It succeeded the Carrera GT and was produced in a limited run of 918 units, in keeping with its name. Its most defining feature was its plug-in hybrid powertrain. The mid-mounted 4.6-liter V-8 engine, producing 599.6 HP, was paired with two electric motors on the front axle and one on the rear, delivering a combined system output of up to 873.8 HP.
car3459.hero: This super sports car represents the first plug-in hybrid flagship from the famed German car maker.

car3462.desc: Introduced in 1968, the second-generation Pontiac GTO was hailed as a pioneer of the muscle car era, though it faced fierce competition. To silence the debate, Pontiac unveiled “The Judge." Equipped with a 6.6-liter Ram Air III V-8, a Hurst shifter, heavy-duty suspension, wide tires, and a rear spoiler, the package propelled the GTO back to the forefront of the muscle car wars.
car3462.hero: The ultimate sports spec car that appeared towards the end of the GTO era, when muscle cars flourished.

car3464.desc: In the early 1950s, the American sports car market was largely ruled by European imports. It was during this time that Chevrolet introduced the original Corvette. The first models featured a forward-thinking design, combining a steel frame with lightweight fiberglass body panels. Power came from a 3.8-liter inline-6 producing 149.9 HP. Initially built as a limited run of just 300 units, the Corvette quickly captured public interest, leading to full-scale production beginning in 1954. That year, output was increased slightly to 152.9 HP, and by 1958, the Corvette gained distinctive quad headlights.
car3464.hero: The origin of the American sports car: the glorious first-generation Corvette.

car3466.desc: The Sierra RS Cosworth was created in 1995 by the masters at Cosworth. Originally a family car, the Sierra’s 2L inline-4 engine was fully tuned, adding a DOHC head and turbocharger, along with other chassis upgrades. The Sierra RS500 Cosworth was introduced a year later. Between 1988 and 1990, it competed in Group A category races around the world, winning several championship titles.
car3466.hero: A Cosworth tuned masterpiece that dominated touring car racing.

car3467.desc: The fifth-generation Civic Type R made its debut in 2017. While previous models focused on enhancing the base Civic’s performance, the fifth-generation Type R was developed in parallel with the standard model from the ground up. In 2020, the lineup was further refined with the introduction of the Limited Edition model. Weight was reduced by 44 lbs through the removal of soundproofing materials and the adoption of specially forged wheels. Subtle suspension tweaks were also made to sharpen handling. With only 1,000 units produced worldwide, the Limited Edition sold out almost immediately.
car3467.hero: What will no doubt be a collector car someday, the limited-edition Civic Type R sold out in minutes.
car3467.nameLong: Honda Civic Type R Limited Edition (FK8) '20

car3468.desc: This RUF original was based on the 991-generation Porsche 911 GT3. Developed with the philosophy of blending GT3-level performance with refined road car comfort, it was powered by a naturally-aspirated Mezger engine—fitted with the legendary GT1 crankshaft—and enlarged from 3.8 to 4.2 liters. Riveted overfenders added a bold visual statement, emphasizing the car’s raw capability and presence. A true enthusiast’s machine, tailored for the gentleman driver.
car3468.hero: The ultimate naturally-aspirated flat-6 machine, meticulously crafted by Ruf.

car3469.desc: The Ferrari F8 Tributo was unveiled in 2019 as the successor to the 488 GTB. While it retained a shape similar to its predecessor, significant changes to the aerodynamic elements gave it a refreshed, aggressive character. Its twin-turbo 3.9-liter V-8 produced 710.1 HP, resulting in a zero-to-62.1 mph of 2.9 seconds and a top speed of 211.3 mph—making it the fastest V-8-powered road car Ferrari had ever produced. Equipped with the latest in body control systems, the F8 Tributo also offered remarkable ease of drivability.
car3469.hero: At the heart of this exotic, an update to the 488GTB, is a powerful V-8 that was also in the 488 Pista.

car3470.desc: The Ferrari 812 Superfast, introduced in 2017, carried on the company's tradition of front-engined V-12 grand tourers. It marked Ferrari’s first use of electric power steering and adopted an evolved version of the 4-wheel steering system from the F12berlinetta. Despite its substantial 107.1 inches wheelbase, the car remained impressively agile through tight corners.
car3470.hero: Adopting the classic V-12 FR layout, this Ferrari possesses remarkable performance while retaining practicality.

car3471.desc: The sixth-generation Toyota Celica made its debut in October 1993. Its futuristic design was sharpened by the distinctive quad round headlights, while a larger body emphasized its identity as a front-wheel-drive specialty car. In 1994, the GT-FOUR (ST205) appeared as a homologation model for the WRC. Its 3S-GTE turbocharged 2.0-liter engine produced 251.5 HP.
car3471.hero: This is the WRC base model of the popular sporty coupe, complete with aluminum hood and rear spoiler.

car3473.desc: The Chiron is a super sports car by Bugatti, introduced in 2016. Limited to a global production run of just 500 units, it serves as the spiritual successor to the groundbreaking Veyron. Built around a carbon-fiber chassis with rigidity comparable to that of an LMP1 race car, the Chiron is powered by the Veyron’s quad-turbo 8.0-liter W16, tuned to produce 1479.3 HP and 1179.7 ft-lb of torque. It can accelerate from zero to 62.1 mph in just 2.5 seconds, and a prototype version recorded a top speed of 304.8 mph.
car3473.hero: The successor to the ultra-high-performance Veyron.

car3474.desc: Starting in 2012, Subaru entered the BRZ into Japan’s domestic Super GT series, competing in the GT300 class. After the release of the second-generation BRZ in 2021, Subaru transitioned to a new GT machine based on the updated model. The new car retained proven elements like the EJ20 engine, while incorporating enhancements to weight distribution and aerodynamics. That same year, the BRZ claimed the GT300 class championship, marking a historic first for Subaru.
car3474.hero: Cornering better than ever before. A BRZ for the Super GT.

car3475.desc: This McLaren race car contested the 1988 F1 World Championship. Its chassis, the work of Gordon Murray and Steve Nichols, was paired with the Honda RA168E powerplant. Dominating the season, it triumphed in 15 of the 16 races. Car No. 12, the MP4/4, was piloted by Ayrton Senna. Senna delivered a stellar performance, securing 13 pole positions and 8 victories en route to the drivers' championship title.
car3475.hero: This legendary machine marked the end of the turbocharged era in Formula 1.

car3476.desc: The SUZUKI Vision Gran Turismo harnesses the cutting-edge engine technology of the renowned Hayabusa sports bike, paired with advanced electrification and weight-saving innovations. Its powertrain combines the 1,340 cm³ (1340 cc) Hayabusa engine with three high-output electric motors in an all-wheel-drive layout. Together, they deliver a total system output of 426 HP at 9700 rpm, making this compact machine a true super sports car.
car3476.hero: A super sports car combining the heart of the Hayabusa with electric motors.

car3477.desc: The seventh-generation S15 Silvia marked a return to the more compact proportions of the S13, reestablishing itself as an accessible, rear-wheel-drive sports car. While it continued to use the SR20 engine from previous generations, its chassis and running gear underwent a comprehensive redesign. With improved body rigidity, upgraded brakes, a more aggressive suspension setup, and the addition of a helical LSD, the S15 delivered a higher level of performance than its predecessors.
car3477.hero: This popular S15 model included side skirts and a rear spoiler.
car3477.nameLong: Nissan Silvia spec-R Aero (S15) Touring Car

car3478.desc: This lightweight, hyper-performance machine honored Porsche’s storied legacy while offering a glimpse into the future of sports cars. Its exterior and interior flowed together in perfect harmony, delivering an exceptionally immersive driving experience. Power came from twin electric motors, while an innovative active aerodynamic system adjusted in real time to deliver optimal downforce and efficiency for any condition.
car3478.hero: Porsche's modern yet daring statement on the future of the sports car remains true to its racing roots.

car3479.desc: Jaguar’s third Vision Gran Turismo paid homage to the iconic Jaguar D-type. This futuristic electric open single-seater with an aero screen is powered by three electric motors generating more than 986.2 HP. Behind the seat is a modern take on the D-type’s signature fin, while the focused, minimalist cockpit controls reflected Jaguar’s storied racing legacy.
car3479.hero: A roadster that's an heir to the legendary D-Type.

car3480.desc: This is the Gr.4 version of the KATANA Edition concept, a fusion of the ZC33 Swift Sport and the striking style and performance of the iconic KATANA sports bike. Enhancements include an extended front under spoiler and the addition of a GT-style rear wing, With staggered tire sizing, interior weight reduction, and the installation of a roll cage, the machine has been transformed into a true Gran Turismo Gr.4-spec race car.
car3480.hero: A tuned up Gr. 4 version of the Swift Sport based on the 'KATANA Edition'.
car3480.nameLong: Suzuki Swift Sport KATANA Edition Gr.4

car3481.desc: Toyota’s lightweight 86, a front-engine/rear-wheel-drive sports car, was introduced in 2012 and sold more than 200,000 units worldwide. Nine years later, it was reborn as the GR86, now equipped with a larger naturally-aspirated 2.4-liter flat-4 DOHC engine producing 231.8 HP and 184.4 ft-lb of torque. With enhanced body rigidity, reduced weight, and an aerodynamic design shaped by motorsport experience, the GR86 delivered an even more engaging and dynamic driving experience.
car3481.hero: This version of Japan's signature lightweight sports car boasts a bigger engine, but it remains true to its heritage.

car3482.desc: The V40 was a 5-door hatchback positioned in the C-segment. Drawing inspiration from Volvo classics of the 1960s—such as the P1800 and 1800ES—its flowing silhouette blended cues of both a coupe and a wagon. The T5 R-Design was the sportiest model in the lineup. Powered by a turbocharged 2.0-liter inline-5 producing 210.1 HP, it was paired with a sport suspension and 18-inch wheels to deliver sharp, refined handling.
car3482.hero: The globally successful Volvo that served as a sedan, estate and coupe.

car3483.desc: This ferocious beast housed the S55 twin-turbo 3.0-liter inline-6 from the M3 and M4 within the compact body of the 2 Series coupe. Its flared fenders hinted at the performance lurking beneath, and a brief press of the throttle was all it took to unleash the full force as the turbochargers came alive. The suspension incorporated aluminum components to reduce unsprung weight. Meanwhile, the torque-vectoring Active M Differential allowed it to tackle any corner with confidence and precision.
car3483.hero: A hardboiled FR that hides the power of a demon in its compact body.

car3485.desc: It represents one of the ultimate evolutions derived from the AMG GT lineage since its debut in 2014. Its 4.0-liter V-8 has been specially tuned to deliver an impressive 719.9 HP and 800 Nm (590.0 ft-lb) of torque. The suspension system has been completely reengineered with upgraded materials and construction, optimizing handling and cornering precision. Adding to its appeal is aggressive, race-inspired bodywork.
car3485.hero: This ultimate version of the AMG GT is laden with Formula 1 technology.

car3486.desc: In 2008, Dodge revived the Challenger nameplate for a new third generation, honoring the legacy of the original muscle car icon. Since its return, several high-performance variants have been introduced, but the standout came in 2018. The SRT Demon was an uncompromising machine built for drag racing dominance. Tuned to deliver 840.2 HP on 100-octane or higher fuel, the Demon could storm through the quarter mile in a jaw-dropping 9.65 seconds.
car3486.hero: A Demon born simply to run the quarter mile as fast as possible.

car3487.desc: This enhanced variant was exclusively offered on the 1969 and 1970 model years of Ford’s original Mustang. Built for NASCAR homologation, this Mustang housed the largest engine ever fitted to the model—a 7.0-liter V-8 known as the 429. Easily identified by its prominent hood scoop, it is often hailed as the most powerful Mustang in the model’s storied history.
car3487.hero: This special high-performance Mustang was produced for only two years.

car3488.desc: The Cayman GT4 joined the Porsche Cayman lineup in 2015 as a motorsports-focused model. It was powered by a 3.8-liter flat-6 derived from the 911 Carrera S, paired with a 6-speed manual transmission. With an output of 379.7 HP, it surpassed the base 911 Carrera in performance and incorporated braking and suspension components from the 991-generation 911 GT3. Optional equipment included a roll cage and 6-point harnesses.
car3488.hero: A Cayman designed for motorsports and possessing all the competitive flair of the 911.

car3489.desc: The Maserati A6GCS/53 Spyder earned the Gran Turismo Trophy at the 2014 Pebble Beach Concours d'Elegance. Its elegant aluminum bodywork was crafted by Carrozzeria Fantuzzi, while power came from a 167.7 HP engine designed by Gioacchino Colombo. Raced under the official Maserati factory team, it secured five class victories and three overall wins during the 1954 season.
car3489.hero: A beautiful streamlined 2-seat sports car that won the Gran Turismo Trophy

car3490.desc: In 1963, Porsche developed the Carrera GTS in response to the World Sportscar Championship regulations of the era. To meet the 100-unit production homologation requirement, the car employed a ladder-frame chassis paired with a lightweight fiberglass body. It delivered strong performance and achieved numerous victories, beginning with the Targa Florio, ultimately becoming the foundation of Porsche’s GT racing efforts throughout the 1960s.
car3490.hero: A masterpiece that brought great success to Porsche's GT race efforts in the 1960s

car3493.desc: The Skyline Super Silhouette was a silhouette formula race car—built using only the basic outline of the production model—based on the sixth-generation Skyline. Its aggressive bodywork featured flared front and rear fenders and a large rear wing, and powered by a turbocharged 2.1-liter LZ20B inline-4 race engine. Between 1982 and 1984, this car secured an impressive eight victories.
car3493.hero: An extraordinary Skyline that stood out in races of the 1980s

car3494.desc: Since its original launch in 2002, the Toyota Alphard had continuously aimed to define the luxury minivan segment. The third-generation Alphard, launched in 2015, introduced the Executive Lounge trim, delivering exceptional comfort to second-row passengers. It offered a higher level of luxury and refinement than ever before. A 2017 facelift brought updates to the 4.5-liter V-6 engine and further enhancements to overall ride comfort.
car3494.hero: Japan's premium minivan that evolved into a high-class luxury car.

car3495.desc: This rotary sports-car concept was unveiled at the 2015 Tokyo Motor Show. Every unnecessary line and surface were meticulously carved away from its sleek long-nose, short-deck silhouette, revealing Mazda’s purest interpretation of the ideal rear-wheel-drive sports car. Powered by the next-generation SKYACTIV-R rotary engine, this concept offered a bold glimpse into the future of rotary performance.
car3495.hero: This stunning concept provided a glimpse of a next-generation rotary-engine-powered car.

car3499.desc: The TOYOTA GR010 HYBRID 2021 succeeded the TS050, developed in response to the new regulations introduced that year. It featured a twin-turbo 3.5-liter V-6 engine producing 670.6 HP, paired with a 268.2 HP electric motor at the front in a 4-wheel-drive layout. Driver lineups including Kamui Kobayashi and Kazuki Nakajima went on to win all six rounds of the WEC season, including Le Mans, ushering in the beginning of the hypercar era.
car3499.hero: Four consecutive wins at Le Mans for Toyota with this prototype race car

car3500.desc: Introduced in 2017, the Genesis G70 sports sedan marked the brand’s entry-level offering. It came with three powertrain options: a 3.3-liter twin-turbo V-6 producing 364.9 HP, a turbocharged 2.0-liter gasoline, and a 2.2-liter turbodiesel. A major facelift followed in 2020, incorporating design cues from Genesis’ flagship models. In 2021, a shooting brake variant—offered exclusively in Europe—further elevated the G70’s appeal.
car3500.hero: An AWD Genesis sports sedan powered by a potent twin-turbo V-6.

car3501.desc: As the entry point to the Genesis lineup, the G70 plays a key role in introducing drivers to the brand’s appeal. Its design was refreshed in 2020 with styling cues from flagship models, and in 2021, a sleek shooting brake variant was launched exclusively for the European market. The Genesis G70 GR4 is a Gran Turismo-spec machine, finely tuned for Gr.4 competition.
car3501.hero: An AWD Genesis sports sedan powered by a potent twin-turbo V-6.

car3502.desc: In April 2021, Genesis revealed its vision for the future of grand touring with the Genesis X Concept. Showcasing the brand’s "Athletic Elegance" design language, it featured the signature crest grille and clean, straight body lines. The Genesis X GR3 carries this design philosophy into the world of motorsports. This innovative Gr.3 machine embodies the fusion of luxury and racing prowess.
car3502.hero: A Gr.3 machine that combines luxury with competition performance.

car3504.desc: The production model of the seventh-generation Fairlady Z first appeared in prototype form in 2020. Eschewing electrification, Nissan opted for the VR30DDTT twin-turbo 3.0-liter V-6, paired with either a 6-speed manual transmission or a 9-speed automatic with manual shift mode. At a time when the automotive industry was shifting toward self-driving technology and electrification, this car pursued the timeless allure of a front-engine/rear-wheel-drive sports car.
car3504.hero: The seventh-generation Z is a 21st century reinterpretation of the classic S30.

car3506.desc: The Toyota 86 and Subaru BRZ, both rear-wheel drive sports cars powered by boxer engines, were developed through a close collaboration between Toyota and Subaru. The series evolved into its second generation with the ZD8 in 2020. The updated platform featured a lighter yet more rigid body, while the engine was an all-new 2.4-liter boxer unit. Its peak output reached 231.8 HP. The Subaru BRZ "S" grade was positioned as a premium trim, offering enhanced interior and exterior appointments.
car3506.hero: The second-gen FR sports car features a larger 2.4-liter engine.

car3507.desc: It was the Spyder variant of the Porsche Vision Gran Turismo, which originally made its debut in 2021. The sculpted surfaces and refined cabin fused artfully to heighten driver engagement. Beneath it all, the dual-motor setup and active aero system worked in concert to ensure performance remained as precise as it was exhilarating.
car3507.hero: Porsche's modern-yet-daring statement on the future of the sports car.

car3508.desc: The SUZUKI Vision Gran Turismo harnesses the cutting-edge engine technology of the renowned Hayabusa sports bike, paired with advanced electrification and weight-saving innovations. Its powertrain combines the 1,340 cm³ (1340 cc) Hayabusa engine with three high-output electric motors in an all-wheel-drive layout. Together, they deliver a total system output of 426 HP at 9700 rpm, making this compact machine a true super sports car.
car3508.hero: This Gr.3 Vision Gran Turismo possesses Suzuki's racing spirit.

car3509.desc: The first Porsche 911 to carry the RS badge was the 911 Carrera RS 2.7, released in 1973. The "RS" stood for Rennsport, meaning racing sport in German. Developed to meet FIA Group 4 homologation requirements, the car was designed with motorsports in mind. It quickly proved to be a hit—its initial production run of 500 units sold out immediately. Due to high demand, Porsche expanded production, ultimately building a total of 1,580 examples.
car3509.hero: A first in Porsche 911 history, the elusive Rennsport.

car3510.desc: The Ferrari Vision Gran Turismo marks Ferrari’s first-ever virtual-only single-seater concept, drawing design cues from the marque’s legendary sports prototypes of the 1960s and 1970s. Its turbocharged 3.0-liter V-6 hybrid powertrain, working in concert with three electric motors, delivers a total system output of 1015.8 HP. Blending the DNA of Ferrari’s past icons with a bold vision of endurance racing’s future, the design is both a tribute and a statement.
car3510.hero: A single-seat concept that pushes the boundaries of the hypercar genre.

car3511.desc: Volkswagen’s prototype race car stood as a symbol of carbon reduction and future performance. Its carbon-fiber body featured prominent front and rear wings, while two electric motors powered both the front and rear axles for all-wheel drive. The car delivered astonishing performance, setting record-breaking times at Pikes Peak, the Nürburgring Nordschleife, and Goodwood.
car3511.hero: The prototype EV that rewrote speed records around the world.

car3512.desc: This motorsport-focused base model was introduced as part of the fourth-generation Roadster lineup. Its drivetrain was upgraded to meet the demands of track use, complemented by a larger radiator and enhanced disc brakes. The suspension featured height-adjustable dampers supplied by Bilstein. In 2022, the car received Kinematic Posture Control, designed to dramatically improve rear-end stability and cornering composure.
car3512.hero: This motorsports-based model epitomizes the core concepts of the Roadster.

car3513.desc: The broader stance of the S14-generation Silvia lent it a more upscale, refined presence. Under the hood, it retained the SR20 engine from the S13, with the top-grade K’s model receiving an added boost from an intercooled turbocharger.
